As I remember, Adam, it was upon this fashion bequeathed me by will but / poor a thousand crowns, and, as thou sayst, charged my brother, on his / blessing, to breed me well; and there begins my sadness. My brother / Jaques he keeps at school, and report speaks goldenly of his profit. / For my part, he keeps me rustically at home, or, to speak more / properly, stays me here at home unkept; for call you that keeping, for / a gentleman of my birth, that differs not from the stalling of an ox? / His horses are bred better, for, besides that they are fair with their / feeding, they are taught their manage and to that end riders dearly / hired; but I, his brother, gain nothing under him but growth, for the / which his animals on his dunghills are as much bound to him as I. / Besides this nothing that he so plentifully gives me, the something / that nature gave me his countenance seems to take from me. He lets me / feed with his hinds, bars me the place of a brother, and as much as in / him lies, mines my gentility with my education. This is it, Adam, that / grieves me, and the spirit of my father, which I think is within me, / begins to mutiny against this servitude. I will no longer endure it, / though yet I know no wise remedy how to avoid it.

As I remember it, Adam, this is how it was. My father left me in his will a mere thousand crowns and, as you say, ordered my brother, on pain of losing his blessing, to bring me up well. That's where my unhappiness begins. My brother Jaques he keeps at university, and everyone speaks glowingly of how well he's doing. As for me, he keeps me at home like a peasant, or, to put it more exactly, he keeps me here without keeping me at all. Do you call it keeping a gentleman of my birth, when it's no different from stabling an ox? His horses are better brought up: as well as being well fed, they're trained in their paces, and he pays riders good money to do it. But I, his brother, get nothing from him except growing bigger, and his animals on his dunghills owe him as much for that as I do. On top of this nothing that he gives me so generously, his treatment of me seems to take away the something that nature gave me. He makes me eat with his farmhands, denies me a brother's place, and does all he can to ruin my gentle birth through my lack of education. That's what grieves me, Adam. And my father's spirit, which I think is inside me, is starting to rebel against this slavery. I won't put up with it any longer, though I still don't know a sensible way to escape it.
Yonder comes my master, your brother.
Here comes my master, your brother.
Go apart, Adam, and thou shalt hear how he will shake me up.
Stand aside, Adam, and you'll hear how he bullies me.
Now, sir, what make you here?
Now, sir, what are you making here?
Nothing. I am not taught to make anything.
Nothing. I've never been taught to make anything.
Then what are you spoiling, sir?
Marry, sir, I am helping you to mar that which God made, a poor / unworthy brother of yours, with idleness.
Well, sir, I'm helping you to spoil what God made, your poor worthless brother, by keeping him idle.
Marry, sir, be better employed, and be naught awhile.
Well, sir, find something better to do, and be off with you.
Shall I keep your hogs, and eat husks with them? What prodigal portion / have I spent that I should come to such penury?
Shall I look after your pigs and eat their husks with them? What inheritance have I wasted, like the Prodigal Son, that I should be brought so low?
Know you where you are, sir?
Do you know where you are, sir?
O, sir, very well: here in your orchard.
Oh yes, sir, very well: here in your orchard.
Do you know who you're standing in front of, sir?

Ay, better than him I am before knows me. I know you are my eldest / brother, and in the gentle condition of blood you should so know me. / The courtesy of nations allows you my better in that you are the / first-born, but the same tradition takes not away my blood, were there / twenty brothers betwixt us. I have as much of my father in me as you, / albeit I confess your coming before me is nearer to his reverence.

Yes, better than the man I'm standing in front of knows me. I know you're my eldest brother, and since we share noble blood you should recognise me as your brother too. Custom puts you above me because you were born first, but that same custom doesn't take away my blood, even if there were twenty brothers between us. I have as much of our father in me as you do, though I admit that, being born before me, you come closer to the respect he was owed.
Come, come, elder brother, you are too young in this.
Come on, elder brother, you're too young to try that.
Wilt thou lay hands on me, villain?
Are you going to lay hands on me, you villain?

I am no villain. I am the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys; he was / my father, and he is thrice a villain that says such a father begot / villains. Wert thou not my brother, I would not take this hand from thy / throat till this other had pulled out thy tongue for saying so. Thou / has railed on thyself.

I am no villain. I'm the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys. He was my father, and anyone who says such a father fathered villains is three times a villain himself. If you weren't my brother, I wouldn't take this hand off your throat until this other one had pulled your tongue out for saying so. You've insulted yourself.
[Coming forward] Sweet masters, be patient. For your father's / remembrance, be at accord.
Dear masters, be patient. For the sake of your father's memory, make peace.
Let me go, I tell you.

I will not till I please. You shall hear me. My father charged you in / his will to give me good education. You have trained me like a peasant, / obscuring and hiding from me all gentleman-like qualities. The spirit / of my father grows strong in me, and I will no longer endure it. / Therefore allow me such exercises as may become a gentleman, or give me / the poor allottery my father left me by testament; with that I will go / buy my fortunes.

Not until I'm ready. You'll listen to me. Our father ordered you in his will to give me a good education. You've brought me up like a peasant, keeping from me all the accomplishments of a gentleman. My father's spirit grows strong in me, and I won't put up with it any longer. So either let me train in the things a gentleman should, or give me the small share my father left me in his will, and I'll go and seek my fortune with it.
And what wilt thou do? Beg when that is spent? Well, sir, get you in. I / will not long be troubled with you. You shall have some part of your / will. I pray you leave me.
And what will you do? Beg when that's spent? Well, sir, go inside. I won't be bothered with you much longer. You'll have some of what you want. Now please leave me.
I no further offend you than becomes me for my good.
I won't trouble you any more than I need to for my own good.
Get you with him, you old dog.
Go with him, you old dog.
Is "old dog" my reward? Most true, I have lost my teeth in your / service. God be with my old master. He would not have spoke such a / word.
Is 'old dog' my reward? It's true, I've lost my teeth in your service. God rest my old master. He would never have said such a thing.
Is it even so? Begin you to grow upon me? I will physic your rankness, / and yet give no thousand crowns neither. Holla, Dennis!
Is that how it is? Are you starting to outgrow me? I'll cure your insolence, and without paying out the thousand crowns either. Hey, Dennis!
Was not Charles, the Duke's wrestler, here to speak with me?
Hasn't Charles, the Duke's wrestler, been here to speak to me?
So please you, he is here at the door and importunes access to you.
If you please, he's at the door now, asking to see you.
'Twill be a good way, and tomorrow the wrestling is.
This will be a good way to do it, and the wrestling is tomorrow.
Good Monsieur Charles. What's the new news at the new court?
Good Monsieur Charles. What's the new news at the new court?

There's no news at the court, sir, but the old news. That is, the old / Duke is banished by his younger brother the new Duke, and three or four / loving lords have put themselves into voluntary exile with him, whose / lands and revenues enrich the new Duke; therefore he gives them good / leave to wander.

There's no news at court, sir, except the old news. That is, the old Duke has been banished by his younger brother, the new Duke, and three or four loyal lords have gone into exile with him of their own free will. Their lands and income go to the new Duke, so he's happy to let them wander.
Can you tell if Rosalind, the Duke's daughter, be banished with her / father?
Can you tell me whether Rosalind, the old Duke's daughter, has been banished with her father?

O, no; for the Duke's daughter, her cousin, so loves her, being ever / from their cradles bred together, that she would have followed her / exile or have died to stay behind her. She is at the court and no less / beloved of her uncle than his own daughter, and never two ladies loved / as they do.

Oh, no. The new Duke's daughter, her cousin, loves her so much, having been brought up with her from the cradle, that she would have followed her into exile or died if she'd been left behind. She's at court, and her uncle loves her as much as his own daughter. Never have two girls loved each other the way they do.
Where will the old Duke live?
Where will the old Duke live?

They say he is already in the Forest of Arden, and a many merry men / with him; and there they live like the old Robin Hood of England. They / say many young gentlemen flock to him every day and fleet the time / carelessly, as they did in the golden world.

They say he's already in the Forest of Arden, and a lot of merry men with him, and that they live there like Robin Hood of old England. They say many young gentlemen join him every day and pass the time without a care, as people did in the golden age.
What, you wrestle tomorrow before the new Duke?
So, you're wrestling tomorrow in front of the new Duke?

Marry, do I, sir, and I came to acquaint you with a matter. I am given, / sir, secretly to understand that your younger brother Orlando hath a / disposition to come in disguised against me to try a fall. Tomorrow, / sir, I wrestle for my credit, and he that escapes me without some / broken limb shall acquit him well. Your brother is but young and / tender, and for your love I would be loath to foil him, as I must for / my own honour if he come in. Therefore, out of my love to you, I came / hither to acquaint you withal, that either you might stay him from his / intendment, or brook such disgrace well as he shall run into, in that / it is a thing of his own search and altogether against my will.

Yes, sir, I am, and I've come to tell you something. I've been told in secret, sir, that your younger brother Orlando means to come in disguise and take me on. Tomorrow, sir, I'm wrestling for my reputation, and anyone who gets away from me without a broken limb will have done well. Your brother is only young and inexperienced, and for your sake I'd hate to throw him, as I'll have to for my own honour if he steps in. So, out of my regard for you, I came to warn you, so that you can either stop him or accept the disgrace he'll suffer, since he's brought it on himself and it's entirely against my wishes.

Charles, I thank thee for thy love to me, which thou shalt find I will / most kindly requite. I had myself notice of my brother's purpose / herein, and have by underhand means laboured to dissuade him from it; / but he is resolute. I'll tell thee, Charles, it is the stubbornest / young fellow of France, full of ambition, an envious emulator of every / man's good parts, a secret and villainous contriver against me his / natural brother. Therefore use thy discretion. I had as lief thou didst / break his neck as his finger. And thou wert best look to't; for if thou / dost him any slight disgrace, or if he do not mightily grace himself on / thee, he will practise against thee by poison, entrap thee by some / treacherous device, and never leave thee till he hath ta'en thy life by / some indirect means or other. For I assure thee (and almost with tears / I speak it) there is not one so young and so villainous this day / living. I speak but brotherly of him, but should I anatomize him to / thee as he is, I must blush and weep, and thou must look pale and / wonder.

Charles, thank you for your concern for me, which I'll repay very generously. I'd heard of my brother's plan myself and have quietly tried to talk him out of it, but he's determined. I'll tell you this, Charles: he's the most stubborn young man in France, full of ambition, jealous of everyone's good qualities, and secretly plotting against me, his own brother. So do as you see fit. I'd be just as happy for you to break his neck as his finger. And you'd better watch out. If you disgrace him even slightly, or if he doesn't win a great triumph over you, he'll plot against you with poison, trap you with some treacherous trick, and never leave you alone until he's killed you one way or another. I assure you (and I say it almost in tears) there is no one alive today so young and so wicked. I'm speaking kindly of him, as a brother; if I described him to you as he really is, I'd blush and weep and you'd turn pale with amazement.
I am heartily glad I came hither to you. If he come tomorrow I'll give / him his payment. If ever he go alone again I'll never wrestle for prize / more. And so, God keep your worship.
I'm very glad I came to you. If he comes tomorrow I'll give him what he deserves. If he ever walks without help again, I'll never wrestle for a prize again. And so, God keep your worship.

Farewell, good Charles. Now will I stir this gamester. I hope I shall / see an end of him; for my soul—yet I know not why—hates nothing more / than he. Yet he's gentle, never schooled and yet learned, full of noble / device, of all sorts enchantingly beloved, and indeed so much in the / heart of the world, and especially of my own people, who best know him, / that I am altogether misprized. But it shall not be so long; this / wrestler shall clear all. Nothing remains but that I kindle the boy / thither, which now I'll go about.

Goodbye, good Charles. Now I'll stir up this young sportsman. I hope I'll see the end of him, because my soul, though I don't know why, hates nothing more than him. Yet he's well-bred, never schooled and yet learned, full of noble ideas, adored by people of every kind, and in fact so loved by everyone, and especially by my own servants, who know him best, that I'm completely undervalued. But it won't be like that for long; this wrestler will settle everything. All I have to do is fire the boy up to go, and I'll do that now.
I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my coz, be merry.
Please, Rosalind, my sweet cousin, cheer up.

Dear Celia, I show more mirth than I am mistress of, and would you yet / I were merrier? Unless you could teach me to forget a banished father, / you must not learn me how to remember any extraordinary pleasure.
Dear Celia, I'm already showing more happiness than I feel, and you want me to be merrier still? Unless you can teach me to forget a banished father, you can't teach me to remember any great joy.

Herein I see thou lov'st me not with the full weight that I love thee. / If my uncle, thy banished father, had banished thy uncle, the Duke my / father, so thou hadst been still with me, I could have taught my love / to take thy father for mine. So wouldst thou, if the truth of thy love / to me were so righteously tempered as mine is to thee.

That shows me you don't love me as much as I love you. If my uncle, your banished father, had banished your uncle, the Duke my father, and you'd still been with me, I could have taught my love to take your father as my own. So would you, if your love for me were as true as mine is for you.
Well, I will forget the condition of my estate to rejoice in yours.
Well, I'll forget my own situation and enjoy yours.

You know my father hath no child but I, nor none is like to have; and / truly, when he dies thou shalt be his heir, for what he hath taken away / from thy father perforce, I will render thee again in affection. By / mine honour I will! And when I break that oath, let me turn monster. / Therefore, my sweet Rose, my dear Rose, be merry.

You know my father has no child but me, and isn't likely to have any. And truly, when he dies you'll be his heir, because what he took from your father by force I'll give back to you out of love. On my honour I will! And if I break that promise, let me turn into a monster. So, my sweet Rose, my dear Rose, be merry.
From henceforth I will, coz, and devise sports. Let me see—what think / you of falling in love?
From now on I will, cousin, and think up games. Let me see. What do you think of falling in love?
Marry, I prithee do, to make sport withal; but love no man in good / earnest, nor no further in sport neither than with safety of a pure / blush thou mayst in honour come off again.
Yes, please do, as a game; but don't love any man seriously, and don't go further, even in fun, than you can get out of again safely with nothing worse than an innocent blush.
What shall be our sport, then?
Then what shall our game be?
Let us sit and mock the good housewife Fortune from her wheel, that her / gifts may henceforth be bestowed equally.
Let's sit and mock that good housewife Fortune away from her spinning wheel, so that from now on she hands out her gifts fairly.
I would we could do so, for her benefits are mightily misplaced, and / the bountiful blind woman doth most mistake in her gifts to women.
I wish we could, because her gifts are badly misplaced, and the generous blind woman makes most mistakes when she gives to women.
'Tis true, for those that she makes fair she scarce makes honest, and / those that she makes honest she makes very ill-favouredly.
That's true, because the women she makes beautiful she hardly ever makes chaste, and the ones she makes chaste she makes very ugly.
Nay, now thou goest from Fortune's office to Nature's. Fortune reigns / in gifts of the world, not in the lineaments of Nature.
No, now you're moving from Fortune's job to Nature's. Fortune rules worldly gifts, not people's features, which come from Nature.

No? When Nature hath made a fair creature, may she not by Fortune fall / into the fire? Though Nature hath given us wit to flout at Fortune, / hath not Fortune sent in this fool to cut off the argument?

Doesn't she? When Nature has made a beautiful creature, can't Fortune make her fall into the fire? Nature may have given us wit to mock Fortune, but hasn't Fortune sent this fool in to cut our argument short?
Indeed, there is Fortune too hard for Nature, when Fortune makes / Nature's natural the cutter-off of Nature's wit.
Indeed, Fortune is too strong for Nature there, when she uses Nature's born fool to cut off Nature's wit.

Peradventure this is not Fortune's work neither, but Nature's, who / perceiveth our natural wits too dull to reason of such goddesses, and / hath sent this natural for our whetstone; for always the dullness of / the fool is the whetstone of the wits.—How now, wit, whither wander / you?

Perhaps this isn't Fortune's doing either, but Nature's. She sees our natural wits are too dull to argue about such goddesses, so she's sent this born fool to sharpen them on, since a fool's dullness is always the whetstone of wit. Hello, wit! Where are you wandering?
Mistress, you must come away to your father.
Mistress, you must come to your father.
Have they made you the messenger?
No, by mine honour, but I was bid to come for you.
No, on my honour, but I was told to come and fetch you.
Where learned you that oath, fool?
Where did you learn that oath, fool?

Of a certain knight that swore by his honour they were good pancakes, / and swore by his honour the mustard was naught. Now, I'll stand to it, / the pancakes were naught and the mustard was good, and yet was not the / knight forsworn.

From a certain knight who swore on his honour that the pancakes were good, and swore on his honour the mustard was no good. Now, I'll swear the pancakes were no good and the mustard was good, and yet the knight hadn't broken his oath.
How prove you that in the great heap of your knowledge?
How do you prove that, from your great heap of knowledge?
Ay, marry, now unmuzzle your wisdom.
Yes, go on, unmuzzle your wisdom.
Stand you both forth now: stroke your chins, and swear by your beards / that I am a knave.
Both of you step forward. Stroke your chins and swear by your beards that I'm a rogue.
By our beards, if we had them, thou art.
By our beards, if we had any, you are.

By my knavery, if I had it, then I were. But if you swear by that that / is not, you are not forsworn. No more was this knight swearing by his / honour, for he never had any; or if he had, he had sworn it away before / ever he saw those pancackes or that mustard.

By my roguery, if I had any, I would be. But if you swear by something that doesn't exist, you haven't broken your oath. Nor had this knight, swearing by his honour, because he never had any, or if he had, he'd sworn it all away before he ever saw those pancakes or that mustard.
Prithee, who is't that thou mean'st?
Tell me, who do you mean?
One that old Frederick, your father, loves.
Someone old Frederick, your father, is fond of.
My father's love is enough to honour him. Enough! Speak no more of him. / You'll be whipped for taxation one of these days.
My father's affection is enough to make him honourable. Enough! Say no more about him. You'll be whipped for your slander one of these days.
The more pity that fools may not speak wisely what wise men do / foolishly.
It's a shame that fools aren't allowed to speak wisely about the foolish things wise men do.
By my troth, thou sayest true. For since the little wit that fools have / was silenced, the little foolery that wise men have makes a great show. / Here comes Monsieur Le Beau.
Honestly, you're right. Since the little wit that fools have was silenced, the little foolishness that wise men have makes a big show. Here comes Monsieur Le Beau.
With his mouth full of news.
With his mouth full of news.
Which he will put on us as pigeons feed their young.
Which he'll push into us the way pigeons feed their young.
Then we'll be stuffed with news.
All the better; we shall be the more marketable. / Bonjour, Monsieur Le Beau. What's the news?
So much the better: we'll fetch a better price at market, like fattened birds. Good day, Monsieur Le Beau. What's the news?
Fair princess, you have lost much good sport.
Fair princess, you've missed some good sport.
What colour, madam? How shall I answer you?
What kind, madam? How shall I answer you?
However your wit and luck allow.
Well said. That was laid on with a trowel.
Well said. That was laid on thick.
Nay, if I keep not my rank—
No, if I don't keep up my rank as a wit...
You'll lose your old smell. ('Rank' also means stinking.)
You amaze me, ladies. I would have told you of good wrestling, which / you have lost the sight of.
You bewilder me, ladies. I meant to tell you about some good wrestling that you've missed seeing.
Yet tell us the manner of the wrestling.
Tell us how the wrestling went, then.
I will tell you the beginning and, if it please your ladyships, you may / see the end, for the best is yet to do; and here, where you are, they / are coming to perform it.
I'll tell you how it started, and, if your ladyships like, you can see the end, because the best is still to come; and right here, where you're standing, they're coming to do it.
Well, the beginning that is dead and buried.
Well then, the beginning, which is dead and buried.
There comes an old man and his three sons—
There comes an old man and his three sons...
I could match this beginning with an old tale.
I could match that beginning with an old fairy tale.
Three proper young men of excellent growth and presence.
Three fine young men, well grown and good-looking.
With bills on their necks: "Be it known unto all men by these / presents."
With notices hung round their necks: 'Be it known to all men by these presents.' (She puns on 'presence'.)

The eldest of the three wrestled with Charles, the Duke's wrestler, / which Charles in a moment threw him and broke three of his ribs, that / there is little hope of life in him. So he served the second, and so / the third. Yonder they lie, the poor old man their father making such / pitiful dole over them that all the beholders take his part with / weeping.

The eldest of the three wrestled with Charles, the Duke's wrestler, and Charles threw him in a moment and broke three of his ribs, so that there's little hope he'll live. He did the same to the second, and to the third. There they lie, and the poor old man, their father, is grieving so pitifully over them that everyone watching is weeping on his side.
But what is the sport, monsieur, that the ladies have lost?
But what's the sport, monsieur, that the ladies have missed?
Why, this that I speak of.
Why, what I've just told you.
Thus men may grow wiser every day. It is the first time that ever I / heard breaking of ribs was sport for ladies.
So men may grow wiser every day. That's the first time I've ever heard that breaking ribs was sport for ladies.
But is there any else longs to see this broken music in his sides? Is / there yet another dotes upon rib-breaking? Shall we see this wrestling, / cousin?
But is there anyone else who wants to hear this broken music in his sides? Is there anyone else who loves rib-breaking? Shall we watch this wrestling, cousin?
You must if you stay here, for here is the place appointed for the / wrestling, and they are ready to perform it.
You'll have to if you stay here, because this is the place chosen for the wrestling, and they're ready to start.
Yonder, sure, they are coming. Let us now stay and see it.
Look, they're definitely coming. Let's stay and watch.
Come on. Since the youth will not be entreated, his own peril on his / forwardness.
Come on. Since the young man won't be talked out of it, let his rashness be his own risk.
Is that the man over there?
Alas, he is too young. Yet he looks successfully.
Oh dear, he's too young. But he looks as though he might win.
How now, daughter and cousin? Are you crept hither to see the / wrestling?
Well, daughter and niece? Have you crept out here to watch the wrestling?
Ay, my liege, so please you give us leave.
Yes, my lord, if you'll allow us.

You will take little delight in it, I can tell you, there is such odds / in the man. In pity of the challenger's youth I would fain dissuade / him, but he will not be entreated. Speak to him, ladies; see if you can / move him.

You won't enjoy it much, I can tell you, the odds against him are so great. I'd like to talk the challenger out of it because he's so young, but he won't listen. Speak to him, ladies, and see if you can persuade him.
Call him hither, good Monsieur Le Beau.
Call him over, good Monsieur Le Beau.
Do so; I'll not be by.
Monsieur the challenger, the Princess calls for you.
Monsieur challenger, the princesses are calling for you.
I attend them with all respect and duty.
I'll come to them with all respect and duty.
Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?
Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?
No, fair princess. He is the general challenger. I come but in as / others do, to try with him the strength of my youth.
No, fair princess. He's the one who challenges everyone. I'm only coming in like the others, to test the strength of my youth against him.

Young gentleman, your spirits are too bold for your years. You have / seen cruel proof of this man's strength. If you saw yourself with your / eyes or knew yourself with your judgement, the fear of your adventure / would counsel you to a more equal enterprise. We pray you for your own / sake to embrace your own safety and give over this attempt.

Young gentleman, your spirit is too bold for your age. You've seen cruel proof of this man's strength. If you could see yourself with your own eyes and judge yourself clearly, fear of the danger would advise you to take on a more even match. We beg you, for your own sake, to think of your safety and give this up.
Do, young sir. Your reputation shall not therefore be misprized. We / will make it our suit to the Duke that the wrestling might not go / forward.
Do, young sir. Your reputation won't suffer for it. We'll ask the Duke ourselves to stop the wrestling.

I beseech you, punish me not with your hard thoughts, wherein I confess / me much guilty to deny so fair and excellent ladies anything. But let / your fair eyes and gentle wishes go with me to my trial, wherein if I / be foiled there is but one shamed that was never gracious; if killed, / but one dead that is willing to be so. I shall do my friends no wrong, / for I have none to lament me; the world no injury, for in it I have / nothing. Only in the world I fill up a place, which may be better / supplied when I have made it empty.

Please don't punish me by thinking badly of me, though I admit I'm very wrong to refuse such lovely and excellent ladies anything. But let your lovely eyes and kind wishes go with me into my contest. If I'm beaten, only someone who never had any favour is shamed; if I'm killed, only someone who's willing to die is dead. I'll do my friends no wrong, because I have none to mourn me; and the world no harm, because I have nothing in it. In the world I only fill up a place, which may be better filled when I've left it empty.
The little strength that I have, I would it were with you.
I wish the little strength I have were with you.
And mine to eke out hers.
And mine, to add to hers.
Fare you well. Pray heaven I be deceived in you.
Goodbye. I pray to heaven I'm wrong about you (and you win).
Your heart's desires be with you.
May you get what your heart desires.
Come, where is this young gallant that is so desirous to lie with his / mother earth?
Come on, where's this young show-off who's so eager to lie down with his mother earth?
Ready, sir; but his will hath in it a more modest working.
Here, sir; but he has a more modest aim than that.
You shall try but one fall.
No, I warrant your grace you shall not entreat him to a second, that / have so mightily persuaded him from a first.
No, I promise your grace you won't need to beg him to try a second, when you tried so hard to talk him out of the first.
You mean to mock me after; you should not have mocked me before. But / come your ways.
You mean to mock me afterwards; you shouldn't mock me beforehand. But come on.
Now, Hercules be thy speed, young man!
Now may Hercules help you, young man!
I would I were invisible, to catch the strong fellow by the leg.
I wish I were invisible, so I could grab that strong fellow by the leg.
If I had a thunderbolt in mine eye, I can tell who should down.
If I had a thunderbolt in my eye, I know who would go down.
Yes, I beseech your grace. I am not yet well breathed.
Yes, please, your grace. I'm not even warmed up yet.
What is thy name, young man?
Orlando, my liege, the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.
Orlando, my lord, the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.

I would thou hadst been son to some man else. / The world esteemed thy father honourable, / But I did find him still mine enemy. / Thou shouldst have better pleased me with this deed / Hadst thou descended from another house. / But fare thee well, thou art a gallant youth. / I would thou hadst told me of another father.

I wish you'd been some other man's son. The world thought your father honourable, but I always found him my enemy. You'd have pleased me more with this feat if you came from another family. But goodbye; you're a brave young man. I wish you'd named another father.
Were I my father, coz, would I do this?
If I were my father, cousin, would I behave like this?
I am more proud to be Sir Rowland's son, / His youngest son, and would not change that calling / To be adopted heir to Frederick.
I'm prouder to be Sir Rowland's son, his youngest son, and I wouldn't give up that name to be Frederick's adopted heir.

My father loved Sir Rowland as his soul, / And all the world was of my father's mind. / Had I before known this young man his son, / I should have given him tears unto entreaties / Ere he should thus have ventured.

My father loved Sir Rowland as his own soul, and the whole world agreed with my father. If I'd known before that this young man was his son, I'd have added tears to my pleas before I let him take such a risk.

Gentle cousin, / Let us go thank him and encourage him. / My father's rough and envious disposition / Sticks me at heart.—Sir, you have well deserved. / If you do keep your promises in love / But justly, as you have exceeded promise, / Your mistress shall be happy.

Dear cousin, let's go and thank him and encourage him. My father's harsh and spiteful temper wounds me to the heart. Sir, you've done very well. If you keep your promises in love as faithfully as you've gone beyond what you promised here, the woman you love will be happy.
Wear this for me—one out of suits with Fortune, / That could give more but that her hand lacks means.— / Shall we go, coz?
Wear this for me. I'm someone out of favour with Fortune, who would give more if her hand had the means. Shall we go, cousin?
Can I not say, I thank you? My better parts / Are all thrown down, and that which here stands up / Is but a quintain, a mere lifeless block.
Can't I even say 'thank you'? My best qualities are all thrown down, and what's left standing here is just a target dummy, a lifeless block of wood.
He calls us back. My pride fell with my fortunes. / I'll ask him what he would.—Did you call, sir?— / Sir, you have wrestled well and overthrown / More than your enemies.
He's calling us back. My pride fell with my fortunes; I'll ask him what he wants. Did you call, sir? Sir, you've wrestled well, and overthrown more than your enemies.
What passion hangs these weights upon my tongue? / I cannot speak to her, yet she urged conference. / O poor Orlando, thou art overthrown. / Or Charles or something weaker masters thee.
What feeling hangs these weights on my tongue? I couldn't speak to her, though she invited me to talk. Oh, poor Orlando, you've been overthrown! Either Charles or something weaker has mastered you.

Good sir, I do in friendship counsel you / To leave this place. Albeit you have deserved / High commendation, true applause, and love, / Yet such is now the Duke's condition / That he misconsters all that you have done. / The Duke is humorous; what he is indeed / More suits you to conceive than I to speak of.

Good sir, as a friend I advise you to leave this place. Although you've earned high praise, real applause and love, the Duke is in such a mood that he misinterprets everything you've done. The Duke is moody; what he's really like is better for you to imagine than for me to say.
I thank you, sir; and pray you tell me this: / Which of the two was daughter of the Duke / That here was at the wrestling?
Thank you, sir. And please tell me this: which of the two who were here at the wrestling was the Duke's daughter?

Neither his daughter, if we judge by manners, / But yet indeed the smaller is his daughter. / The other is daughter to the banished Duke, / And here detained by her usurping uncle / To keep his daughter company, whose loves / Are dearer than the natural bond of sisters. / But I can tell you that of late this Duke / Hath ta'en displeasure 'gainst his gentle niece, / Grounded upon no other argument / But that the people praise her for her virtues / And pity her for her good father's sake; / And, on my life, his malice 'gainst the lady / Will suddenly break forth. Sir, fare you well. / Hereafter, in a better world than this, / I shall desire more love and knowledge of you.

Neither is his daughter, if we judge by behaviour; but in fact the shorter one is his daughter. The other is the banished Duke's daughter, kept here by her usurping uncle to keep his daughter company, and the two love each other more dearly than sisters by birth. But I can tell you that lately this Duke has taken against his gentle niece, for no other reason than that the people praise her for her virtues and pity her for her good father's sake. And, on my life, his malice against the lady will soon break out. Sir, goodbye. Some day, in a better world than this, I'll want to know you better and be your friend.
I rest much bounden to you; fare you well!
I'm very much in your debt. Goodbye!
Thus must I from the smoke into the smother, / From tyrant Duke unto a tyrant brother. / But heavenly Rosalind!
So I must go out of the smoke into the stifling fire, from a tyrant Duke to a tyrant brother. But heavenly Rosalind!
Why, cousin, why, Rosalind! Cupid have mercy! Not a word?
Cousin! Rosalind! Cupid have mercy! Not a word?
Not one to throw at a dog.
Not one I'd throw to a dog.
No, thy words are too precious to be cast away upon curs. Throw some of / them at me. Come, lame me with reasons.
No, your words are too precious to throw away on curs. Throw some at me. Come on, lame me with reasons.
Then there were two cousins laid up, when the one should be lamed with / reasons and the other mad without any.
Then there'd be two cousins laid up: one lamed with reasons and the other driven mad without any.
But is all this for your father?
But is all this for your father?
No, some of it is for my child's father. O, how full of briers is this / working-day world!
No, some of it is for my child's father (the man I'd like to marry). Oh, how full of thorns this everyday world is!
They are but burs, cousin, thrown upon thee in holiday foolery. If we / walk not in the trodden paths, our very petticoats will catch them.
They're only burrs, cousin, thrown at you in holiday fun. If we walk off the beaten paths, our petticoats will catch them.
I could shake them off my coat; these burs are in my heart.
I could shake them off my coat. These burrs are in my heart.
I would try, if I could cry "hem" and have him.
I would try, if I could cry 'hem' and have him.
Come, come, wrestle with thy affections.
Come on, wrestle with your feelings.
O, they take the part of a better wrestler than myself.
Oh, they're on the side of a better wrestler than me.

O, a good wish upon you! You will try in time, in despite of a fall. / But turning these jests out of service, let us talk in good earnest. Is / it possible on such a sudden you should fall into so strong a liking / with old Sir Rowland's youngest son?

Oh, good luck to you! You'll take him on in time, even if you have a fall. But let's dismiss these jokes and talk seriously. Is it possible that you've suddenly fallen so deeply for old Sir Rowland's youngest son?
The Duke my father loved his father dearly.
The Duke my father loved his father dearly.
Doth it therefore ensue that you should love his son dearly? By this / kind of chase I should hate him, for my father hated his father dearly; / yet I hate not Orlando.
Does it follow that you should love his son dearly? By that logic I should hate him, because my father hated his father dearly. Yet I don't hate Orlando.
No, faith, hate him not, for my sake.
No, really, don't hate him, for my sake.
Why should I not? Doth he not deserve well?
Why shouldn't I? Doesn't he deserve it?
Let me love him for that, and do you love him because I do.—Look, here / comes the Duke.
Let me love him for that, and you love him because I do. Look, here comes the Duke.
With his eyes full of anger.
With his eyes full of anger.
Mistress, dispatch you with your safest haste, / And get you from our court.
Madam, get ready as fast as you safely can, and leave our court.
You, cousin. / Within these ten days if that thou be'st found / So near our public court as twenty miles, / Thou diest for it.
You, niece. If you're found within twenty miles of our court in the next ten days, you'll die for it.

I do beseech your Grace, / Let me the knowledge of my fault bear with me. / If with myself I hold intelligence, / Or have acquaintance with mine own desires, / If that I do not dream, or be not frantic— / As I do trust I am not—then, dear uncle, / Never so much as in a thought unborn / Did I offend your Highness.

I beg your grace, let me take with me the knowledge of what I've done wrong. If I know my own mind and understand my own wishes, if I'm not dreaming or mad, as I trust I'm not, then, dear uncle, I have never offended your highness even in a half-formed thought.
Thus do all traitors. / If their purgation did consist in words, / They are as innocent as grace itself. / Let it suffice thee that I trust thee not.
That's what all traitors say. If they could clear themselves with words, they'd all be as innocent as heaven itself. It's enough that I don't trust you.
Yet your mistrust cannot make me a traitor. / Tell me whereon the likelihood depends.
But your distrust can't make me a traitor. Tell me what your suspicion is based on.
Thou art thy father's daughter, there's enough.
You're your father's daughter. That's enough.

So was I when your highness took his dukedom; / So was I when your highness banished him. / Treason is not inherited, my lord, / Or, if we did derive it from our friends, / What's that to me? My father was no traitor. / Then, good my liege, mistake me not so much / To think my poverty is treacherous.

So I was when your highness took his dukedom; so I was when your highness banished him. Treason isn't inherited, my lord; or, even if we did inherit it from our family, what's that to do with me? My father was no traitor. So, my good lord, don't misjudge me so badly as to think that my poverty makes me treacherous.
Ay, Celia, we stayed her for your sake, / Else had she with her father ranged along.
Yes, Celia, we kept her here for your sake; otherwise she'd have gone wandering with her father.

I did not then entreat to have her stay; / It was your pleasure and your own remorse. / I was too young that time to value her, / But now I know her. If she be a traitor, / Why, so am I. We still have slept together, / Rose at an instant, learned, played, ate together, / And wheresoe'er we went, like Juno's swans, / Still we went coupled and inseparable.

I didn't beg you to let her stay then. It was your own wish and your own pity. I was too young then to value her, but now I know her. If she's a traitor, then so am I. We've always slept together, got up at the same moment, studied, played and eaten together, and wherever we went, like Juno's swans, we went as a pair, never apart.

She is too subtle for thee, and her smoothness, / Her very silence, and her patience / Speak to the people, and they pity her. / Thou art a fool. She robs thee of thy name, / And thou wilt show more bright and seem more virtuous / When she is gone. Then open not thy lips. / Firm and irrevocable is my doom / Which I have passed upon her. She is banished.

She's too clever for you. Her gentleness, her very silence and her patience speak to the people, and they pity her. You're a fool. She robs you of your reputation, and you'll shine more brightly and seem more virtuous when she's gone. So don't open your mouth. The sentence I've passed on her is firm and can't be changed. She is banished.
Pronounce that sentence then on me, my liege. / I cannot live out of her company.
Then pass that sentence on me too, my lord. I can't live without her company.
You are a fool. You, niece, provide yourself. / If you outstay the time, upon mine honour / And in the greatness of my word, you die.
You're a fool. You, niece, get ready. If you stay past the deadline, on my honour and by the power of my word, you die.
O my poor Rosalind, whither wilt thou go? / Wilt thou change fathers? I will give thee mine. / I charge thee, be not thou more grieved than I am.
Oh, my poor Rosalind, where will you go? Will you swap fathers? I'll give you mine. I order you, don't be more upset than I am.
I have more reason to be.
Thou hast not, cousin. / Prithee be cheerful. Know'st thou not the Duke / Hath banished me, his daughter?
You don't, cousin. Please cheer up. Don't you realise the Duke has banished me, his daughter?

No, hath not? Rosalind lacks then the love / Which teacheth thee that thou and I am one. / Shall we be sundered? Shall we part, sweet girl? / No, let my father seek another heir. / Therefore devise with me how we may fly, / Whither to go, and what to bear with us, / And do not seek to take your change upon you, / To bear your griefs yourself and leave me out. / For, by this heaven, now at our sorrows pale, / Say what thou canst, I'll go along with thee.

Hasn't he? Then Rosalind lacks the love that would teach you that you and I are one. Shall we be torn apart? Shall we part, sweet girl? No, let my father find another heir. So plan with me how we can escape, where to go and what to take with us. And don't try to take your misfortune on yourself alone, bearing your griefs and leaving me out. I swear by this sky, now pale at our sorrows, whatever you say, I'm going with you.
To seek my uncle in the Forest of Arden.
To find my uncle in the Forest of Arden.
Alas, what danger will it be to us, / Maids as we are, to travel forth so far? / Beauty provoketh thieves sooner than gold.
But how dangerous will it be for us, young women as we are, to travel so far? Beauty tempts thieves even faster than gold does.
I'll put myself in poor and mean attire, / And with a kind of umber smirch my face. / The like do you; so shall we pass along / And never stir assailants.
I'll dress myself in poor, humble clothes and smear my face with brown earth. You do the same; then we'll get through without attracting attackers.

Were it not better, / Because that I am more than common tall, / That I did suit me all points like a man? / A gallant curtal-axe upon my thigh, / A boar-spear in my hand, and in my heart / Lie there what hidden woman's fear there will, / We'll have a swashing and a martial outside, / As many other mannish cowards have / That do outface it with their semblances.

Wouldn't it be better, since I'm unusually tall, if I dressed completely like a man? With a fine cutlass at my side and a boar-spear in my hand, then whatever woman's fear lies hidden in my heart, we'll put on a swaggering, soldierly outside, like plenty of other mannish cowards who bluff it out with their looks.
What shall I call thee when thou art a man?
What shall I call you when you're a man?
I'll have no worse a name than Jove's own page, / And therefore look you call me Ganymede. / But what will you be called?
I'll have nothing less than the name of Jove's own page, so make sure you call me Ganymede. But what will you be called?
Something that hath a reference to my state: / No longer Celia, but Aliena.
Something that fits my situation: no longer Celia, but Aliena (the stranger).
But, cousin, what if we assayed to steal / The clownish fool out of your father's court? / Would he not be a comfort to our travel?
But, cousin, what if we tried to steal the clownish fool away from your father's court? Wouldn't he be a comfort on our journey?

He'll go along o'er the wide world with me. / Leave me alone to woo him. Let's away, / And get our jewels and our wealth together, / Devise the fittest time and safest way / To hide us from pursuit that will be made / After my flight. Now go we in content / To liberty, and not to banishment.

He'd follow me all over the world. Leave it to me to persuade him. Let's go and gather our jewels and money together, and work out the best time and safest way to hide from the search that will be made after I've gone. Now let's go happily, to freedom and not to banishment.

Now, my co-mates and brothers in exile, / Hath not old custom made this life more sweet / Than that of painted pomp? Are not these woods / More free from peril than the envious court? / Here feel we not the penalty of Adam, / The seasons' difference, as the icy fang / And churlish chiding of the winter's wind, / Which when it bites and blows upon my body / Even till I shrink with cold, I smile and say: / "This is no flattery. These are counsellors / That feelingly persuade me what I am." / Sweet are the uses of adversity, / Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous, / Wears yet a precious jewel in his head; / And this our life, exempt from public haunt, / Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks, / Sermons in stones, and good in everything.

Now, my companions and brothers in exile, hasn't long habit made this life sweeter than one of showy splendour? Aren't these woods freer from danger than the jealous court? Here we don't feel Adam's punishment, the change of the seasons, like the icy fang and rough scolding of the winter wind. When it bites and blows on my body until I shrink with cold, I smile and say, 'This isn't flattery. These are advisers that make me feel what I really am.' Hardship has its sweet uses: like the toad, which is ugly and poisonous but wears a precious jewel in its head. And this life of ours, away from the crowds, finds tongues in trees, books in running streams, sermons in stones, and good in everything.
I would not change it. Happy is your grace, / That can translate the stubbornness of fortune / Into so quiet and so sweet a style.
I wouldn't change it. Your grace is lucky to be able to translate the hardness of fortune into such a calm and sweet way of life.

Come, shall we go and kill us venison? / And yet it irks me the poor dappled fools, / Being native burghers of this desert city, / Should in their own confines with forked heads / Have their round haunches gored.

Come, shall we go and kill some deer for food? And yet it troubles me that the poor dappled fools, the natural citizens of this wild city, should have their round haunches pierced by arrows in their own territory.

Indeed, my lord, / The melancholy Jaques grieves at that, / And in that kind swears you do more usurp / Than doth your brother that hath banished you. / Today my lord of Amiens and myself / Did steal behind him as he lay along / Under an oak, whose antique root peeps out / Upon the brook that brawls along this wood; / To the which place a poor sequestered stag, / That from the hunter's aim had ta'en a hurt, / Did come to languish; and indeed, my lord, / The wretched animal heaved forth such groans / That their discharge did stretch his leathern coat / Almost to bursting, and the big round tears / Coursed one another down his innocent nose / In piteous chase. And thus the hairy fool, / Much marked of the melancholy Jaques, / Stood on th' extremest verge of the swift brook, / Augmenting it with tears.

Indeed, my lord, the melancholy Jaques grieves about that, and swears that in this way you're a worse usurper than your brother who banished you. Today Lord Amiens and I crept up behind him as he lay stretched out under an oak whose ancient root sticks out over the stream that babbles through this wood. To that place a poor stag, cut off from the herd, which had been wounded by a hunter, came to die. And truly, my lord, the wretched animal let out such groans that they stretched its leather hide almost to bursting, and big round tears chased one another down its innocent nose in a pitiful race. And so the hairy fool, closely watched by the melancholy Jaques, stood at the very edge of the swift stream, adding to it with its tears.
But what said Jaques? / Did he not moralize this spectacle?
But what did Jaques say? Didn't he draw a moral from the scene?

O yes, into a thousand similes. / First, for his weeping into the needless stream: / "Poor deer," quoth he "thou mak'st a testament / As worldlings do, giving thy sum of more / To that which had too much." Then, being there alone, / Left and abandoned of his velvet friends: / "'Tis right"; quoth he, "thus misery doth part / The flux of company." Anon a careless herd, / Full of the pasture, jumps along by him / And never stays to greet him. "Ay," quoth Jaques, / "Sweep on, you fat and greasy citizens! / 'Tis just the fashion. Wherefore do you look / Upon that poor and broken bankrupt there?" / Thus most invectively he pierceth through / The body of the country, city, court, / Yea, and of this our life, swearing that we / Are mere usurpers, tyrants, and what's worse, / To fright the animals and to kill them up / In their assigned and native dwelling-place.

Oh yes, a thousand comparisons. First, about its weeping into the stream, which didn't need the water: 'Poor deer,' he said, 'you make your will like worldly men do, giving more to those who already have too much.' Then, about its being alone, abandoned by its velvet-coated friends: 'That's right,' he said, 'misery always cuts people off from the flow of company.' Soon a carefree herd, full of grass, came leaping past it and never stopped to greet it. 'Yes,' said Jaques, 'sweep on, you fat and greasy citizens. That's just the fashion. Why should you look at that poor broken bankrupt there?' So, attacking everything, he cut through the whole of country, city and court, and even this life of ours, swearing that we're nothing but usurpers, tyrants and worse, for frightening the animals and killing them in the home that nature gave them.
And did you leave him in this contemplation?
And did you leave him thinking like this?
We did, my lord, weeping and commenting / Upon the sobbing deer.
We did, my lord, weeping and commenting on the sobbing deer.
Show me the place. / I love to cope him in these sullen fits, / For then he's full of matter.
Show me the place. I love to take him on in these gloomy moods, because then he's full of things to say.
I'll bring you to him straight.
I'll take you to him at once.
Can it be possible that no man saw them? / It cannot be! Some villains of my court / Are of consent and sufferance in this.
Is it possible that no one saw them? It can't be! Some villains at my court must have agreed to this and let it happen.
I cannot hear of any that did see her. / The ladies, her attendants of her chamber, / Saw her abed, and in the morning early / They found the bed untreasured of their mistress.
I can't find anyone who saw her. The ladies who wait on her in her bedroom saw her go to bed, and early in the morning they found the bed empty of its treasure, their mistress.

My lord, the roynish clown, at whom so oft / Your grace was wont to laugh, is also missing. / Hesperia, the princess' gentlewoman, / Confesses that she secretly o'erheard / Your daughter and her cousin much commend / The parts and graces of the wrestler / That did but lately foil the sinewy Charles; / And she believes wherever they are gone / That youth is surely in their company.

My lord, the scurvy clown your grace used to laugh at so often is missing too. Hesperia, the princess's lady-in-waiting, admits she secretly overheard your daughter and her cousin praising the qualities and graces of the wrestler who recently beat the muscular Charles, and she believes that wherever they've gone, that young man is with them.

Send to his brother; fetch that gallant hither. / If he be absent, bring his brother to me. / I'll make him find him. Do this suddenly! / And let not search and inquisition quail / To bring again these foolish runaways.

Send to his brother's house and bring that fine fellow here. If he's not there, bring his brother to me; I'll make him find him. Do it at once! And don't let the search and questioning slacken until these foolish runaways are brought back.

What, my young master? O my gentle master, / O my sweet master, O you memory / Of old Sir Rowland! Why, what make you here? / Why are you virtuous? Why do people love you? / And wherefore are you gentle, strong, and valiant? / Why would you be so fond to overcome / The bonny prizer of the humorous Duke? / Your praise is come too swiftly home before you. / Know you not, master, to some kind of men / Their graces serve them but as enemies? / No more do yours. Your virtues, gentle master, / Are sanctified and holy traitors to you. / O, what a world is this, when what is comely / Envenoms him that bears it!

What, my young master? Oh, my gentle master, my sweet master, you living memory of old Sir Rowland! What are you doing here? Why are you so good? Why do people love you? And why are you noble, strong and brave? Why were you so foolish as to beat the moody Duke's sturdy prizefighter? Your fame has come home too fast, ahead of you. Don't you know, master, that for some men their good qualities only act as their enemies? Yours do the same. Your virtues, gentle master, are holy, sacred traitors to you. Oh, what a world this is, when someone's goodness poisons him!

O unhappy youth, / Come not within these doors! Within this roof / The enemy of all your graces lives. / Your brother—no, no brother, yet the son— / Yet not the son; I will not call him son— / Of him I was about to call his father, / Hath heard your praises, and this night he means / To burn the lodging where you use to lie, / And you within it. If he fail of that, / He will have other means to cut you off; / I overheard him and his practices. / This is no place; this house is but a butchery. / Abhor it, fear it, do not enter it.

Oh, unlucky young man, don't come inside these doors! The enemy of all your good qualities lives under this roof. Your brother (no, not a brother; yet the son; no, not the son, I won't call him the son of the man I was about to call his father) has heard you praised, and tonight he means to burn down the lodging where you usually sleep, with you inside it. If that fails, he has other ways of killing you; I overheard him and his plans. This is no place for you; this house is nothing but a slaughterhouse. Loathe it, fear it, don't go in.
Why, whither, Adam, wouldst thou have me go?
But where do you want me to go, Adam?
No matter whither, so you come not here.
It doesn't matter where, so long as you don't come here.

What, wouldst thou have me go and beg my food, / Or with a base and boisterous sword enforce / A thievish living on the common road? / This I must do, or know not what to do. / Yet this I will not do, do how I can. / I rather will subject me to the malice / Of a diverted blood and bloody brother.

What, do you want me to go and beg for my food, or make a living as a thief on the highway with a common, violent sword? That's what I'd have to do, or else I don't know what to do. But I won't do that, whatever happens. I'd rather put myself at the mercy of a brother whose blood has turned against nature and who wants my blood.

But do not so. I have five hundred crowns, / The thrifty hire I saved under your father, / Which I did store to be my foster-nurse, / When service should in my old limbs lie lame, / And unregarded age in corners thrown. / Take that, and He that doth the ravens feed, / Yea, providently caters for the sparrow, / Be comfort to my age. Here is the gold. / All this I give you. Let me be your servant. / Though I look old, yet I am strong and lusty, / For in my youth I never did apply / Hot and rebellious liquors in my blood, / Nor did not with unbashful forehead woo / The means of weakness and debility. / Therefore my age is as a lusty winter, / Frosty but kindly. Let me go with you. / I'll do the service of a younger man / In all your business and necessities.

Don't do that. I have five hundred crowns, the wages I carefully saved while I served your father, which I put aside to look after me when my old limbs became too weak to serve, and old age was ignored and thrown into a corner. Take it, and may God, who feeds the ravens and provides for the sparrow, comfort me in my old age. Here's the gold. I give you all of it. Let me be your servant. Though I look old, I'm strong and healthy, because when I was young I never filled my blood with hot, rebellious drink, and I never shamelessly chased after the things that weaken and wear you out. So my old age is like a hearty winter, frosty but kind. Let me go with you. I'll do the work of a younger man in all your business and needs.

O good old man, how well in thee appears / The constant service of the antique world, / When service sweat for duty, not for meed. / Thou art not for the fashion of these times, / Where none will sweat but for promotion, / And having that do choke their service up / Even with the having. It is not so with thee. / But, poor old man, thou prun'st a rotten tree, / That cannot so much as a blossom yield / In lieu of all thy pains and husbandry. / But come thy ways, we'll go along together, / And ere we have thy youthful wages spent / We'll light upon some settled low content.

Good old man, how clearly you show the faithful service of the old days, when servants worked out of duty, not for reward. You don't belong to the fashion of these times, when no one will work except for promotion, and once they have it, they stop serving the moment they get it. It isn't like that with you. But, poor old man, you're pruning a rotten tree that can't produce a single blossom in return for all your work and care. But come along, we'll go together, and before we've spent the wages of your youth, we'll find some humble, settled way of living.

Master, go on and I will follow thee / To the last gasp with truth and loyalty. / From seventeen years till now almost fourscore / Here lived I, but now live here no more. / At seventeen years many their fortunes seek, / But at fourscore it is too late a week. / Yet fortune cannot recompense me better / Than to die well and not my master's debtor.

Master, go on, and I'll follow you to my last breath, truly and loyally. From the age of seventeen until now, almost eighty, I've lived here, but I'll live here no more. At seventeen many men go off to seek their fortune, but at eighty it's a bit late. Still, fortune can't reward me better than to let me die well and not owe my master anything.
O Jupiter, how weary are my spirits!
Oh, Jupiter, how weary my spirits are!
I care not for my spirits, if my legs were not weary.
I wouldn't care about my spirits if my legs weren't so weary.

I could find in my heart to disgrace my man's apparel, and to cry like / a woman, but I must comfort the weaker vessel, as doublet and hose / ought to show itself courageous to petticoat. Therefore, courage, good / Aliena.

I could find it in my heart to disgrace my man's clothes and cry like a woman, but I have to comfort the weaker sex, since doublet and hose should show courage to petticoats. So, courage, good Aliena.
I pray you bear with me, I cannot go no further.
Please bear with me. I can't go any further.
For my part, I had rather bear with you than bear you. Yet I should / bear no cross if I did bear you, for I think you have no money in your / purse.
For my part, I'd rather bear with you than carry you. Though I'd bear no cross if I did carry you, because I don't think you've got any money in your purse. (Coins were stamped with a cross.)
Well, this is the forest of Arden.
Well, this is the Forest of Arden.
Ay, now am I in Arden, the more fool I! When I was at home I was in a / better place, but travellers must be content.
Yes, now I'm in Arden, more fool me! When I was at home I was in a better place, but travellers must put up with things.
Ay, be so, good Touchstone. Look you, who comes here? A young man and / an old in solemn talk.
Yes, do, good Touchstone. Look, who's coming? A young man and an old one, talking seriously.
That is the way to make her scorn you still.
That's the way to make her go on scorning you.
O Corin, that thou knew'st how I do love her!
Oh, Corin, if only you knew how much I love her!
I partly guess, for I have loved ere now.
I can partly guess, because I've been in love before.

No, Corin, being old, thou canst not guess, / Though in thy youth thou wast as true a lover / As ever sighed upon a midnight pillow. / But if thy love were ever like to mine— / As sure I think did never man love so— / How many actions most ridiculous / Hast thou been drawn to by thy fantasy?

No, Corin, you're old, you can't guess, though when you were young you were as true a lover as ever sighed on a pillow at midnight. But if your love was ever like mine (and I'm sure no man ever loved like this), how many ridiculous things did your imagination lead you into?
Into a thousand that I have forgotten.

O, thou didst then never love so heartily! / If thou rememb'rest not the slightest folly / That ever love did make thee run into, / Thou hast not loved. / Or if thou hast not sat as I do now, / Wearing thy hearer in thy mistress' praise, / Thou hast not loved. / Or if thou hast not broke from company / Abruptly, as my passion now makes me, / Thou hast not loved. / O Phoebe, Phoebe, Phoebe!

Oh, then you never loved as deeply as I do! If you can't remember the smallest foolish thing love ever made you do, you haven't loved. Or if you haven't sat, as I'm doing now, wearing out your listener by praising your mistress, you haven't loved. Or if you haven't suddenly broken away from your friends, as my passion makes me do now, you haven't loved. Oh, Phoebe, Phoebe, Phoebe!
Alas, poor shepherd, searching of thy wound, / I have by hard adventure found mine own.
Poor shepherd! While probing your wound, by bad luck I've found my own.

And I mine. I remember when I was in love I broke my sword upon a stone / and bid him take that for coming a-night to Jane Smile; and I remember / the kissing of her batlet, and the cow's dugs that her pretty chopped / hands had milked; and I remember the wooing of a peascod instead of / her, from whom I took two cods, and, giving her them again, said with / weeping tears, "Wear these for my sake." We that are true lovers run / into strange capers. But as all is mortal in nature, so is all nature / in love mortal in folly.

And I mine. I remember when I was in love I smashed my sword on a stone and told it to take that for coming at night to see Jane Smile. And I remember kissing the bat she beat the washing with, and the cow's udders her pretty chapped hands had milked. And I remember wooing a pea-pod instead of her, and taking two peas from it, and giving them back to her and saying, with tears, 'Wear these for my sake.' We true lovers get up to strange tricks. But just as everything in nature must die, so every natural thing in love is deadly foolish.
Thou speak'st wiser than thou art ware of.
You speak more wisely than you know.
Nay, I shall ne'er be ware of mine own wit till I break my shins / against it.
No, I'll never be aware of my own wit until I break my shins on it.
Jove, Jove, this shepherd's passion / Is much upon my fashion.
Jove, Jove, this shepherd's passion is very like my own.
And mine, but it grows something stale with me.
And mine, but it's getting a bit stale in my case.
I pray you, one of you question yond man / If he for gold will give us any food. / I faint almost to death.
Please, one of you ask that man if he'll give us any food for money. I'm faint almost to death.
Peace, fool, he's not thy kinsman.
Quiet, fool, he's not one of your family.
Otherwise they'd be very wretched indeed.
Peace, I say.—Good even to you, friend.
Quiet, I tell you. Good evening to you, friend.
And to you, gentle sir, and to you all.
And to you, gentle sir, and to all of you.

I prithee, shepherd, if that love or gold / Can in this desert place buy entertainment, / Bring us where we may rest ourselves and feed. / Here's a young maid with travel much oppressed, / And faints for succour.
Please, shepherd, if kindness or money can buy hospitality in this wild place, take us where we can rest and eat. Here's a young woman worn out by travelling, who's fainting for want of help.

Fair sir, I pity her / And wish, for her sake more than for mine own, / My fortunes were more able to relieve her. / But I am shepherd to another man / And do not shear the fleeces that I graze. / My master is of churlish disposition / And little recks to find the way to heaven / By doing deeds of hospitality. / Besides, his cote, his flocks, and bounds of feed / Are now on sale, and at our sheepcote now, / By reason of his absence, there is nothing / That you will feed on. But what is, come see, / And in my voice most welcome shall you be.

Fair sir, I pity her, and I wish, for her sake more than my own, that I were better able to help her. But I'm shepherd to another man, and I don't shear the sheep I graze. My master is a mean-tempered man, and doesn't care much about finding the way to heaven by doing deeds of hospitality. Besides, his cottage, flocks and grazing land are up for sale now, and because he's away there's nothing at our sheepfold that you'd want to eat. But what there is, come and see; as far as I can say, you're very welcome.
What is he that shall buy his flock and pasture?
Who's going to buy his flock and pasture?
That young swain that you saw here but erewhile, / That little cares for buying anything.
That young lad you saw here a moment ago, who doesn't much care about buying anything.
I pray thee, if it stand with honesty, / Buy thou the cottage, pasture, and the flock, / And thou shalt have to pay for it of us.
Please, if it can be done honestly, you buy the cottage, pasture and flock, and we'll give you the money to pay for it.
And we will mend thy wages. I like this place, / And willingly could waste my time in it.
And we'll raise your wages. I like this place, and I could happily spend my time here.

Assuredly the thing is to be sold. / Go with me. If you like upon report / The soil, the profit, and this kind of life, / I will your very faithful feeder be, / And buy it with your gold right suddenly.

It's certainly for sale. Come with me. If, when you've heard about it, you like the land, the income and this kind of life, I'll be your very faithful shepherd and buy it with your gold straight away.

[Sings] / Under the greenwood tree, / Who loves to lie with me / And turn his merry note / Unto the sweet bird's throat, / Come hither, come hither, come hither! / Here shall he see / No enemy / But winter and rough weather.
Whoever loves to lie with me under the green trees, and tune his cheerful song to the sweet bird's singing, come here, come here, come here! Here he'll see no enemy but winter and rough weather.
It will make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques.
It'll make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques.
I thank it. More, I prithee, more. I can suck melancholy out of a song / as a weasel sucks eggs. More, I prithee, more.
I thank it for that. More, please, more. I can suck melancholy out of a song the way a weasel sucks eggs. More, please, more.
My voice is ragged. I know I cannot please you.
My voice is rough. I know I can't please you.
I do not desire you to please me; I do desire you to sing. Come, more, / another stanzo. Call you 'em stanzos?
I don't want you to please me; I want you to sing. Come on, more, another stanzo. Is that what you call them, stanzos?
Nay, I care not for their names. They owe me nothing. Will you sing?
No, I don't care about their names. They don't owe me any money. Will you sing?
More at your request than to please myself.
More because you ask than to please myself.

Well then, if ever I thank any man, I'll thank you; but that they call / compliment is like th' encounter of two dog-apes. And when a man thanks / me heartily, methinks I have given him a penny and he renders me the / beggarly thanks. Come, sing; and you that will not, hold your tongues.

Well then, if I ever thank any man, I'll thank you. But what people call compliments is like two baboons meeting. And when a man thanks me warmly, I feel as if I've given him a penny and he's giving me a beggar's thanks. Come on, sing; and those of you who won't, hold your tongues.
Well, I'll end the song.—Sirs, cover the while. The Duke will drink / under this tree; he hath been all this day to look you.
Well, I'll finish the song. Gentlemen, lay the table meanwhile. The Duke will drink under this tree. He's been looking for you all day.
And I have been all this day to avoid him. He is too disputable for my / company. I think of as many matters as he, but I give heaven thanks and / make no boast of them. Come, warble, come.
And I've been avoiding him all day. He's too fond of arguing for my liking. I think about as many things as he does, but I thank heaven for them and don't boast about them. Come on, warble, come.

[Sings] / Who doth ambition shun / And loves to live i' th' sun, / Seeking the food he eats / And pleased with what he gets, / Come hither, come hither, come hither. / Here shall he see / No enemy / But winter and rough weather.
Whoever shuns ambition and loves to live in the sun, finding his own food and happy with what he gets, come here, come here, come here. Here he'll see no enemy but winter and rough weather.
I'll give you a verse to this note that I made yesterday in despite of / my invention.
I'll give you a verse to this tune that I made up yesterday, in spite of having no imagination.

Thus it goes: / If it do come to pass / That any man turn ass, / Leaving his wealth and ease / A stubborn will to please, / Ducdame, ducdame, ducdame; / Here shall he see / Gross fools as he, / An if he will come to me.

This is how it goes: If it happens that any man turns into an ass, leaving his wealth and comfort to follow a stubborn whim, ducdame, ducdame, ducdame: here he'll see fools as big as he is, if he'll only come to me.
'Tis a Greek invocation to call fools into a circle. I'll go sleep if I / can; if I cannot, I'll rail against all the first-born of Egypt.
It's a Greek spell for calling fools into a circle. I'll go and sleep if I can. If I can't, I'll rant against all the first-born of Egypt.
And I'll go seek the Duke; his banquet is prepared.
And I'll go and find the Duke. His banquet is ready.
Dear master, I can go no further. O, I die for food! Here lie I down / and measure out my grave. Farewell, kind master.
Dear master, I can't go any further. Oh, I'm dying for food! I'll lie down here and measure out my grave. Goodbye, kind master.

Why, how now, Adam? No greater heart in thee? Live a little, comfort a / little, cheer thyself a little. If this uncouth forest yield anything / savage, I will either be food for it or bring it for food to thee. Thy / conceit is nearer death than thy powers. For my sake, be comfortable. / Hold death awhile at the arm's end. I will here be with thee presently, / and if I bring thee not something to eat, I'll give thee leave to die. / But if thou diest before I come, thou art a mocker of my labour. Well / said, thou look'st cheerly, and I'll be with thee quickly. Yet thou / liest in the bleak air. Come, I will bear thee to some shelter and thou / shalt not die for lack of a dinner if there live anything in this / desert. Cheerly, good Adam!

What's this, Adam? Have you no more courage than that? Live a little, comfort yourself a little, cheer up a little. If this wild forest has any savage animal in it, I'll either be its food or bring it back as food for you. You're closer to death in your mind than in your body. For my sake, cheer up. Hold death off at arm's length for a while. I'll be back with you soon, and if I don't bring you something to eat, I'll give you permission to die. But if you die before I come back, you're mocking all my efforts. Well done, you look more cheerful, and I'll be back quickly. But you're lying in the cold air. Come, I'll carry you to some shelter, and you won't die for lack of a meal if anything lives in this wilderness. Cheer up, good Adam!
I think he be transformed into a beast, / For I can nowhere find him like a man.
I think he must have turned into an animal, because I can't find him anywhere in the shape of a man.
My lord, he is but even now gone hence; / Here was he merry, hearing of a song.
My lord, he's only just left. He was here, cheerful, listening to a song.
If he, compact of jars, grow musical, / We shall have shortly discord in the spheres. / Go seek him, tell him I would speak with him.
If he, who's made entirely of discords, is becoming musical, we'll soon have discord in the music of the spheres. Go and find him, and tell me I want to speak to him.
He saves my labour by his own approach.
He's saved me the trouble by coming himself.
Why, how now, monsieur? What a life is this / That your poor friends must woo your company? / What, you look merrily.
Well, monsieur, what kind of life is this, when your poor friends have to beg for your company? What, you look cheerful!

A fool, a fool! I met a fool i' th' forest, / A motley fool. A miserable world! / As I do live by food, I met a fool, / Who laid him down and basked him in the sun, / And railed on Lady Fortune in good terms, / In good set terms, and yet a motley fool. / "Good morrow, fool," quoth I. "No, sir," quoth he, / "Call me not fool till heaven hath sent me fortune." / And then he drew a dial from his poke, / And, looking on it with lack-lustre eye, / Says very wisely, "It is ten o'clock. / Thus we may see," quoth he, "how the world wags. / 'Tis but an hour ago since it was nine, / And after one hour more 'twill be eleven. / And so from hour to hour we ripe and ripe, / And then from hour to hour we rot and rot, / And thereby hangs a tale." When I did hear / The motley fool thus moral on the time, / My lungs began to crow like chanticleer, / That fools should be so deep-contemplative, / And I did laugh sans intermission / An hour by his dial. O noble fool! / A worthy fool! Motley's the only wear.

A fool, a fool! I met a fool in the forest, a fool in motley. What a miserable world! As sure as I live by food, I met a fool, who lay down and basked in the sun, and cursed Lady Fortune in fine terms, in well-set phrases, and yet he was a motley fool. 'Good morning, fool,' I said. 'No, sir,' he said, 'don't call me fool until heaven has sent me fortune.' (Fortune was said to favour fools.) Then he took a sundial out of his pocket and, looking at it with a dull eye, said very wisely, 'It's ten o'clock. So we can see,' he said, 'how the world goes on. It's only an hour since it was nine, and in one more hour it'll be eleven. And so from hour to hour we ripen and ripen, and then from hour to hour we rot and rot, and there hangs a tale.' When I heard the motley fool moralising like this about time, my lungs began to crow like a rooster that fools could think so deeply, and I laughed without stopping for an hour by his sundial. Oh, noble fool! A worthy fool! Motley is the only thing to wear.

O worthy fool!—One that hath been a courtier, / And says if ladies be but young and fair, / They have the gift to know it. And in his brain, / Which is as dry as the remainder biscuit / After a voyage, he hath strange places crammed / With observation, the which he vents / In mangled forms. O that I were a fool! / I am ambitious for a motley coat.

Oh, a worthy fool! One who's been a courtier, and says that if ladies are young and beautiful, they have the gift of knowing it. And in his brain, which is as dry as the last biscuit left after a voyage, he has odd corners crammed with observations, which he lets out in jumbled forms. Oh, I wish I were a fool! I long for a motley coat.

It is my only suit, / Provided that you weed your better judgements / Of all opinion that grows rank in them / That I am wise. I must have liberty / Withal, as large a charter as the wind, / To blow on whom I please, for so fools have. / And they that are most galled with my folly, / They most must laugh. And why, sir, must they so? / The "why" is plain as way to parish church. / He that a fool doth very wisely hit / Doth very foolishly, although he smart, / Not to seem senseless of the bob.
