If not, / The wise man's folly is anatomized / Even by the squandering glances of the fool. / Invest me in my motley. Give me leave / To speak my mind, and I will through and through / Cleanse the foul body of th' infected world, / If they will patiently receive my medicine.

It's the only suit I'm asking for, provided you weed out of your better judgment any idea, growing wild in it, that I'm wise. I must also have freedom, as wide a licence as the wind, to blow on whoever I like, as fools do. And those who are most stung by my foolery must laugh the most. And why, sir, must they? The reason is as plain as the road to the parish church. The man a fool hits very cleverly would be very foolish, even though it hurts, not to pretend he can't feel the jab. Otherwise the wise man's folly is laid open even by the fool's random shots. Dress me in motley. Give me permission to speak my mind, and I'll cleanse the foul body of this infected world through and through, if they'll take my medicine patiently.
Fie on thee! I can tell what thou wouldst do.
Shame on you! I know what you'd do.
What, for a counter, would I do but good?
What would I do, I'll bet you a penny, but good?

Most mischievous foul sin, in chiding sin; / For thou thyself hast been a libertine, / As sensual as the brutish sting itself, / And all th' embossed sores and headed evils / That thou with license of free foot hast caught / Wouldst thou disgorge into the general world.

Commit the most harmful, filthy sin by criticising sin. You've been a rake yourself, as lustful as the brute instinct itself, and you'd vomit out onto the whole world all the swollen sores and festering diseases you've picked up by wandering freely.

Why, who cries out on pride / That can therein tax any private party? / Doth it not flow as hugely as the sea / Till that the weary very means do ebb? / What woman in the city do I name / When that I say the city-woman bears / The cost of princes on unworthy shoulders? / Who can come in and say that I mean her, / When such a one as she, such is her neighbour? / Or what is he of basest function / That says his bravery is not on my cost, / Thinking that I mean him, but therein suits / His folly to the mettle of my speech? / There then. How then, what then? Let me see wherein / My tongue hath wronged him. If it do him right, / Then he hath wronged himself. If he be free, / Why then my taxing like a wild-goose flies / Unclaimed of any man. But who comes here?

Why, who can attack pride in general and be said to accuse any particular person? Doesn't pride swell as hugely as the sea until the very money that pays for it runs dry? Which woman in the city am I naming when I say that city women carry the wealth of princes on their unworthy shoulders? Who can come forward and say I mean her, when her neighbour is just the same? Or what man of the lowest job, who says his fine clothes weren't paid for by me, thinking that I mean him, isn't just fitting his own folly to the substance of what I say? So there. What then? Let me see how my tongue has wronged him. If it describes him rightly, then he's wronged himself. If he's innocent, then my criticism flies off like a wild goose, claimed by no one. But who's this coming?
Stop, and don't eat any more.
Why, I have eat none yet.
Why, I haven't eaten anything yet.
Nor shalt not till necessity be served.
And you won't, until a man in need is served.
Of what kind should this cock come of?
What breed of fighting cock is this?
Art thou thus boldened, man, by thy distress? / Or else a rude despiser of good manners, / That in civility thou seem'st so empty?
Has your distress made you this bold, man? Or are you a rude despiser of good manners, that you seem to have no courtesy at all?

You touched my vein at first. The thorny point / Of bare distress hath ta'en from me the show / Of smooth civility; yet am I inland bred / And know some nurture. But forbear, I say! / He dies that touches any of this fruit / Till I and my affairs are answered.

You hit the mark the first time. The thorny point of sheer need has robbed me of the outward show of good manners; yet I was brought up in civilised society and know how to behave. But stop, I tell you! Anyone who touches this fruit dies, until I and my needs are seen to.
An you will not be answered with reason, I must die.
If you won't be answered with reason, I'll have to die. (Puns on raisin, the fruit.)
What would you have? Your gentleness shall force / More than your force move us to gentleness.
What do you want? Your gentleness will persuade us more than your force will push us into gentleness.
I almost die for food, and let me have it.
I'm almost dying for food. Let me have some.
Sit down and feed, and welcome to our table.
Sit down and eat, and welcome to our table.

Speak you so gently? Pardon me, I pray you. / I thought that all things had been savage here / And therefore put I on the countenance / Of stern commandment. But whate'er you are / That in this desert inaccessible, / Under the shade of melancholy boughs, / Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time, / If ever you have looked on better days, / If ever been where bells have knolled to church, / If ever sat at any good man's feast, / If ever from your eyelids wiped a tear, / And know what 'tis to pity and be pitied, / Let gentleness my strong enforcement be, / In the which hope I blush and hide my sword.

You speak so gently? Please forgive me. I thought everything here was savage, so I put on a look of stern command. But whoever you are, who, in this unreachable wilderness under the shade of melancholy branches, let the creeping hours slip away unnoticed, if you've ever seen better days, if you've ever been where bells rang for church, if you've ever sat at a good man's feast, if you've ever wiped a tear from your eyes, and know what it is to pity and be pitied, then let gentleness be my strong weapon. In that hope, I blush and put my sword away.

True is it that we have seen better days, / And have with holy bell been knolled to church, / And sat at good men's feasts, and wiped our eyes / Of drops that sacred pity hath engendered. / And therefore sit you down in gentleness, / And take upon command what help we have / That to your wanting may be ministered.

It's true that we've seen better days, and have been called to church by holy bells, and sat at good men's feasts, and wiped from our eyes tears that holy pity has brought. So sit down in peace, and take, as you wish, whatever help we have to meet your needs.

Then but forbear your food a little while, / Whiles, like a doe, I go to find my fawn, / And give it food. There is an old poor man / Who after me hath many a weary step / Limped in pure love. Till he be first sufficed, / Oppressed with two weak evils, age and hunger, / I will not touch a bit.

Then just hold back from your food a little while, while I, like a doe, go to find my fawn and feed it. There's a poor old man who has limped many weary steps after me out of pure love. Until he's been fed first, weighed down as he is by two weakening evils, age and hunger, I won't touch a bite.
Go find him out, / And we will nothing waste till you return.
Go and find him, and we'll eat nothing until you come back.
I thank ye, and be blest for your good comfort.
Thank you, and bless you for your kind help.
Thou seest we are not all alone unhappy. / This wide and universal theatre / Presents more woeful pageants than the scene / Wherein we play in.
You see we're not the only unhappy ones. This wide, universal theatre shows more sorrowful shows than the scene we're acting in.

All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players; / They have their exits and their entrances, / And one man in his time plays many parts, / His acts being seven ages. At first the infant, / Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms; / Then the whining schoolboy, with his satchel / And shining morning face, creeping like snail / Unwillingly to school. And then the lover, / Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad / Made to his mistress' eyebrow. Then a soldier, / Full of strange oaths and bearded like the pard, / Jealous in honour, sudden and quick in quarrel, / Seeking the bubble reputation / Even in the cannon's mouth. And then the justice, / In fair round belly with good capon lined, / With eyes severe and beard of formal cut, / Full of wise saws and modern instances; / And so he plays his part. The sixth age shifts / Into the lean and slippered pantaloon, / With spectacles on nose and pouch on side, / His youthful hose, well saved, a world too wide / For his shrunk shank, and his big manly voice, / Turning again toward childish treble, pipes / And whistles in his sound. Last scene of all, / That ends this strange eventful history, / Is second childishness and mere oblivion, / Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.

The whole world is a stage, and all the men and women are just actors. They have their exits and their entrances, and one man in his lifetime plays many parts, his acts being seven ages. First the baby, whimpering and being sick in the nurse's arms. Then the whining schoolboy, with his satchel and his shining morning face, creeping like a snail unwillingly to school. Then the lover, sighing like a furnace, with a sad song written about his mistress's eyebrow. Then a soldier, full of strange oaths and bearded like a leopard, touchy about his honour, quick to start a fight, chasing a reputation that bursts like a bubble, even into the mouth of a cannon. Then the judge, with a fine round belly lined with good chicken, stern eyes and a neatly trimmed beard, full of wise sayings and everyday examples; and so he plays his part. The sixth age changes into the thin old man in slippers, with spectacles on his nose and a purse at his side. His stockings from his youth, carefully kept, are far too wide for his shrunken legs, and his big manly voice, turning back towards a child's high pitch, pipes and whistles when he speaks. The last scene of all, which ends this strange, eventful story, is a second childhood and complete forgetfulness: without teeth, without eyes, without taste, without everything.
Welcome. Set down your venerable burden, / And let him feed.
Welcome. Put down your respected load, and let him eat.
I thank you most for him.
I thank you most of all for him.
So had you need; / I scarce can speak to thank you for myself.
So you should; I can hardly speak to thank you myself.
Welcome, fall to. I will not trouble you / As yet to question you about your fortunes. / Give us some music, and good cousin, sing.
Welcome, tuck in. I won't bother you yet with questions about your fortunes. Let's have some music. Good cousin, sing.

[Sings] / Blow, blow, thou winter wind, / Thou art not so unkind / As man's ingratitude. / Thy tooth is not so keen, / Because thou art not seen, / Although thy breath be rude. / Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho, unto the green holly. / Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly. / Then, heigh-ho, the holly! / This life is most jolly. / Freeze, freeze, thou bitter sky, / That dost not bite so nigh / As benefits forgot. / Though thou the waters warp, / Thy sting is not so sharp / As friend remembered not. / Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho, unto the green holly. / Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly. / Then, heigh-ho, the holly! / This life is most jolly.

Blow, blow, you winter wind; you're not as unkind as man's ingratitude. Your tooth isn't as sharp, because you can't be seen, though your breath is rough. Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho to the green holly. Most friendship is pretence, most love is just foolishness. Then heigh-ho, the holly! This life is very jolly. Freeze, freeze, you bitter sky; you don't bite as deeply as kindnesses forgotten. Though you turn the waters to ice, your sting isn't as sharp as a friend who's forgotten you. Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho to the green holly. Most friendship is pretence, most love is just foolishness. Then heigh-ho, the holly! This life is very jolly.

If that you were the good Sir Rowland's son, / As you have whispered faithfully you were, / And as mine eye doth his effigies witness / Most truly limned and living in your face, / Be truly welcome hither. I am the Duke / That loved your father. The residue of your fortune / Go to my cave and tell me.—Good old man, / Thou art right welcome as thy master is. / Support him by the arm. [To Orlando] Give me your hand, / And let me all your fortunes understand.

If you're the son of good Sir Rowland, as you've whispered to me truthfully that you are, and as my eye can see his likeness truly drawn and living in your face, then you're truly welcome here. I'm the Duke who loved your father. Come to my cave and tell me the rest of your story. Good old man, you're as welcome as your master is. Support him by the arm. Give me your hand, and let me hear everything that's happened to you.

Not see him since? Sir, sir, that cannot be. / But were I not the better part made mercy, / I should not seek an absent argument / Of my revenge, thou present. But look to it: / Find out thy brother wheresoe'er he is. / Seek him with candle. Bring him dead or living / Within this twelvemonth, or turn thou no more / To seek a living in our territory. / Thy lands, and all things that thou dost call thine / Worth seizure, do we seize into our hands, / Till thou canst quit thee by thy brother's mouth / Of what we think against thee.

Not seen him since? Sir, sir, that can't be true. If I weren't mostly made of mercy, I wouldn't be looking for an absent target for my revenge, with you standing here. But see to it: find your brother, wherever he is. Search for him by candlelight. Bring him back dead or alive within a year, or never come back to make a living in our lands. We are seizing your lands and everything you own that's worth taking, until your brother's own words can clear you of what we suspect you of.
O that your highness knew my heart in this: / I never loved my brother in my life.
Oh, if only your highness knew my heart on this! I've never loved my brother in my life.
More villain thou. Well, push him out of doors, / And let my officers of such a nature / Make an extent upon his house and lands. / Do this expediently, and turn him going.
Then you're all the more a villain. Well, throw him out, and let my officers responsible for such things take possession of his house and lands. Do it quickly, and send him on his way.

Hang there, my verse, in witness of my love. / And thou, thrice-crowned queen of night, survey / With thy chaste eye, from thy pale sphere above, / Thy huntress' name that my full life doth sway. / O Rosalind, these trees shall be my books, / And in their barks my thoughts I'll character, / That every eye which in this forest looks / Shall see thy virtue witnessed everywhere. / Run, run, Orlando, carve on every tree / The fair, the chaste, and unexpressive she.

Hang there, my poem, as proof of my love. And you, queen of the night with three crowns, look down with your chaste eye from your pale orbit above on the name of your huntress, who rules my whole life. Oh, Rosalind, these trees will be my books, and I'll write my thoughts in their bark, so that every eye that looks in this forest will see your goodness proclaimed everywhere. Run, run, Orlando, carve on every tree the beautiful, chaste, indescribable she.
And how like you this shepherd's life, Master Touchstone?
And how do you like this shepherd's life, Master Touchstone?

Truly, shepherd, in respect of itself, it is a good life; but in / respect that it is a shepherd's life, it is naught. In respect that it / is solitary, I like it very well; but in respect that it is private, it / is a very vile life. Now in respect it is in the fields, it pleaseth me / well; but in respect it is not in the court, it is tedious. As it is a / spare life, look you, it fits my humour well; but as there is no more / plenty in it, it goes much against my stomach. Hast any philosophy in / thee, shepherd?

Honestly, shepherd, considered in itself, it's a good life; but considering it's a shepherd's life, it's worthless. Considering it's solitary, I like it very much; but considering it's lonely, it's a very horrible life. Now considering it's in the fields, it pleases me well; but considering it's not at court, it's boring. As it's a simple life, you see, it suits my mood well; but as there's no abundance in it, it goes very much against my stomach. Have you got any philosophy in you, shepherd?

No more but that I know the more one sickens, the worse at ease he is; / and that he that wants money, means, and content is without three good / friends; that the property of rain is to wet, and fire to burn; that / good pasture makes fat sheep; and that a great cause of the night is / lack of the sun; that he that hath learned no wit by nature nor art may / complain of good breeding or comes of a very dull kindred.

No more than this: I know that the sicker you get, the worse you feel; that a man without money, means and contentment lacks three good friends; that rain makes things wet and fire burns; that good pasture makes fat sheep; that a great cause of night is lack of the sun; and that someone who hasn't learned any wit by nature or by study can complain he was badly brought up, or else comes from a very dull family.
Such a one is a natural philosopher. Wast ever in court, shepherd?
A man like that is a natural philosopher (and a born fool). Have you ever been at court, shepherd?
Truly, thou art damned, like an ill-roasted egg, all on one side.
Truly, you're damned, like a badly roasted egg, all done on one side.
For not being at court? Your reason.
For not being at court? Give me your reason.

Why, if thou never wast at court, thou never saw'st good manners; if / thou never saw'st good manners, then thy manners must be wicked, and / wickedness is sin, and sin is damnation. Thou art in a parlous state, / shepherd.

Well, if you've never been at court, you've never seen good manners. If you've never seen good manners, then your manners must be wicked, and wickedness is sin, and sin is damnation. You're in a dangerous state, shepherd.

Not a whit, Touchstone. Those that are good manners at the court are as / ridiculous in the country as the behaviour of the country is most / mockable at the court. You told me you salute not at the court but you / kiss your hands. That courtesy would be uncleanly if courtiers were / shepherds.

Not at all, Touchstone. What's good manners at court is as ridiculous in the country as country behaviour is laughable at court. You told me that at court you don't greet people without kissing your hands. That courtesy would be dirty if courtiers were shepherds.
Give me an example, briefly. Come on, an example.
Why, we are still handling our ewes, and their fells, you know, are / greasy.
Well, we're always handling our ewes, and their fleeces, you know, are greasy.
Why, do not your courtier's hands sweat? And is not the grease of a / mutton as wholesome as the sweat of a man? Shallow, shallow. A better / instance, I say. Come.
Well, don't courtiers' hands sweat? And isn't sheep's grease as wholesome as a man's sweat? Shallow, shallow. A better example, I say. Come on.
Your lips will feel them the sooner. Shallow again. A more sounder / instance, come.
Your lips will feel them all the sooner. Shallow again. A sounder example, come on.
And they are often tarred over with the surgery of our sheep; and would / you have us kiss tar? The courtier's hands are perfumed with civet.
And they're often smeared with tar from treating our sheep's sores. Would you have us kiss tar? Courtiers' hands are perfumed with civet.

Most shallow man! Thou worm's meat in respect of a good piece of flesh / indeed! Learn of the wise and perpend. Civet is of a baser birth than / tar, the very uncleanly flux of a cat. Mend the instance, shepherd.

Most shallow man! You're food for worms compared with a really good piece of meat! Learn from the wise and think about it. Civet has a lower birth than tar: it's the dirty discharge of a cat. Improve your example, shepherd.
You have too courtly a wit for me. I'll rest.
Your wit's too courtly for me. I'll stop.
Wilt thou rest damned? God help thee, shallow man! God make incision in / thee, thou art raw.
Will you stay damned? God help you, shallow man! God cut you open and let some sense in; you're raw.

Sir, I am a true labourer. I earn that I eat, get that I wear, owe no / man hate, envy no man's happiness, glad of other men's good, content / with my harm; and the greatest of my pride is to see my ewes graze and / my lambs suck.

Sir, I'm an honest labourer. I earn what I eat and pay for what I wear. I hate no man, envy no man's happiness, am glad of other men's good luck and put up with my own bad luck; and my greatest pride is to see my ewes graze and my lambs suck.

That is another simple sin in you, to bring the ewes and the rams / together and to offer to get your living by the copulation of cattle; / to be bawd to a bell-wether and to betray a she-lamb of a twelvemonth / to crooked-pated, old, cuckoldly ram, out of all reasonable match. If / thou be'st not damned for this, the devil himself will have no / shepherds. I cannot see else how thou shouldst 'scape.

That's another sin of your simplicity: bringing the ewes and rams together, and making your living from the mating of animals; being a pimp to the lead ram and handing over a year-old female lamb to a crooked-headed old cuckold of a ram, a completely unreasonable match. If you're not damned for this, the devil himself won't have any shepherds. I can't see how else you could escape.
Here comes young Master Ganymede, my new mistress's brother.
Here comes young Master Ganymede, my new mistress's brother.

[Reads] / From the east to western Inde / No jewel is like Rosalind. / Her worth being mounted on the wind, / Through all the world bears Rosalind. / All the pictures fairest lined / Are but black to Rosalind. / Let no face be kept in mind / But the fair of Rosalind.

From the East to the West Indies, no jewel is like Rosalind. Her worth, carried on the wind, takes her name through all the world. All the most beautifully drawn pictures are ugly beside Rosalind. Let no face be remembered except the beauty of Rosalind.
I'll rhyme you so eight years together, dinners and suppers and / sleeping hours excepted. It is the right butter-women's rank to market.
I'll rhyme like that for eight years nonstop, except for dinners, suppers and sleeping hours. It's just like the jogging pace of butter-women riding to market.

For a taste: / If a hart do lack a hind, / Let him seek out Rosalind. / If the cat will after kind, / So be sure will Rosalind. / Winter garments must be lined, / So must slender Rosalind. / They that reap must sheaf and bind, / Then to cart with Rosalind. / Sweetest nut hath sourest rind, / Such a nut is Rosalind. / He that sweetest rose will find / Must find love's prick, and Rosalind. / This is the very false gallop of verses. Why do you infect yourself / with them?

For a taste: if a stag lacks a mate, let him look for Rosalind. If the cat wants its own kind, you can be sure Rosalind will too. Winter clothes have to be lined, and so does slender Rosalind. Those who reap must tie up the sheaves, then onto the cart with Rosalind. The sweetest nut has the sourest rind; Rosalind is a nut like that. Whoever finds the sweetest rose must find love's thorn, and Rosalind. This is the real limping gallop of verse. Why do you infect yourself with it?
Peace, you dull fool, I found them on a tree.
Quiet, you dull fool. I found them on a tree.
Truly, the tree yields bad fruit.
Truly, the tree bears bad fruit.

I'll graft it with you, and then I shall graft it with a medlar. Then / it will be the earliest fruit i' th' country, for you'll be rotten ere / you be half ripe, and that's the right virtue of the medlar.

I'll graft you onto it, and then I'll be grafting it with a medlar. Then it'll be the earliest fruit in the country, because you'll be rotten before you're half ripe, and that's exactly the quality of the medlar.
You have said, but whether wisely or no, let the forest judge.
You've had your say, but whether it was wise or not, let the forest judge.
Peace, here comes my sister, reading. Stand aside.
Quiet, here comes my sister, reading. Stand aside.

[Reads] / Why should this a desert be? / For it is unpeopled? No! / Tongues I'll hang on every tree / That shall civil sayings show. / Some, how brief the life of man / Runs his erring pilgrimage, / That the streching of a span / Buckles in his sum of age; / Some, of violated vows / 'Twixt the souls of friend and friend. / But upon the fairest boughs, / Or at every sentence' end, / Will I "Rosalinda" write, / Teaching all that read to know / The quintessence of every sprite / Heaven would in little show. / Therefore heaven nature charged / That one body should be filled / With all graces wide-enlarged. / Nature presently distilled / Helen's cheek, but not her heart, / Cleopatra's majesty; / Atalanta's better part, / Sad Lucretia's modesty. / Thus Rosalind of many parts / By heavenly synod was devised, / Of many faces, eyes, and hearts / To have the touches dearest prized. / Heaven would that she these gifts should have, / And I to live and die her slave.

Why should this place be a desert? Because no one lives here? No! I'll hang tongues on every tree, to speak wise, civilised sayings. Some will tell how short a man's life is as he wanders on his pilgrimage, so that the width of a hand holds the whole sum of his years; some will tell of broken vows between the souls of friends. But on the finest branches, or at the end of every sentence, I'll write 'Rosalinda', teaching everyone who reads to know that heaven wanted to show in miniature the very essence of every spirit. So heaven ordered nature to fill one body with every grace, spread wide. Nature at once distilled Helen's cheek (but not her faithless heart), Cleopatra's majesty, Atalanta's better part, and sad Lucretia's modesty. So Rosalind was made by a council of the gods out of many parts, to have the best features of many faces, eyes and hearts. Heaven willed that she should have these gifts, and that I should live and die her slave.
O most gentle Jupiter, what tedious homily of love have you wearied / your parishioners withal, and never cried "Have patience, good people!"
Oh, most gentle Jupiter, what a boring sermon of love you've wearied your congregation with, and never once cried 'Be patient, good people!'
How now! Back, friends. Shepherd, go off a little. Go with him, sirrah.
What! Get back, friends. Shepherd, go away a little. Go with him, fellow.
Come, shepherd, let us make an honourable retreat, though not with bag / and baggage, yet with scrip and scrippage.
Come, shepherd, let's make an honourable retreat; not with bag and baggage, like an army, but with our shepherd's pouch and its contents.
O yes, I heard them all, and more too, for some of them had in them / more feet than the verses would bear.
Oh yes, I heard them all, and more besides, because some of them had more feet than the verses could carry.
That's no matter. The feet might bear the verses.
That doesn't matter. The feet might carry the verses.
Ay, but the feet were lame and could not bear themselves without the / verse, and therefore stood lamely in the verse.
Yes, but the feet were lame and couldn't stand up without the verse, so they stood lamely in the verse.
But didst thou hear without wondering how thy name should be hanged and / carved upon these trees?
But did you hear them without wondering how your name came to be hung and carved on these trees?

I was seven of the nine days out of the wonder before you came; for / look here what I found on a palm-tree. I was never so berhymed since / Pythagoras' time that I was an Irish rat, which I can hardly remember.

I was already seven days into the nine-day wonder before you came. Look what I found on a palm tree. I've never been so rhymed about since the time of Pythagoras, when I was an Irish rat, which I can hardly remember. (Rats were supposedly rhymed to death in Ireland.)
Trow you who hath done this?
Can you guess who has done this?
And a chain, that you once wore, about his neck. Change you colour?
With a chain round his neck that you once wore. Are you changing colour?
O Lord, Lord, it is a hard matter for friends to meet; but mountains / may be removed with earthquakes and so encounter.
Oh Lord, Lord, it's hard for friends to meet; but mountains can be moved by earthquakes and so come together.
Nay, I prithee now, with most petitionary vehemence, tell me who it is.
No, I beg you now, as hard as I can beg, tell me who it is.
O wonderful, wonderful, most wonderful wonderful, and yet again / wonderful, and after that, out of all whooping!
Oh, wonderful, wonderful, most wonderful wonderful, and wonderful again, and after that beyond all shouting!

Good my complexion! Dost thou think, though I am caparisoned like a / man, I have a doublet and hose in my disposition? One inch of delay / more is a South Sea of discovery. I prithee tell me who is it quickly, / and speak apace. I would thou couldst stammer, that thou mightst pour / this concealed man out of thy mouth, as wine comes out of / narrow-mouthed bottle—either too much at once or none at all. I prithee / take the cork out of thy mouth that I may drink thy tidings.

For goodness' sake! Do you think that because I'm dressed up like a man I've got a doublet and hose in my nature? One more inch of delay is as long as a voyage of discovery to the South Seas. Please tell me who it is, quickly, and speak fast. I wish you stammered, so that you could pour this hidden man out of your mouth like wine out of a narrow-necked bottle: either too much at once or none at all. Please take the cork out of your mouth so I can drink your news.
So you may put a man in your belly.
So you can put a man in your belly.
Is he of God's making? What manner of man? Is his head worth a hat, or / his chin worth a beard?
Is he made by God? What kind of man? Is his head worth a hat, or his chin worth a beard?
Nay, he hath but a little beard.
No, he's only got a little beard.
Why, God will send more if the man will be thankful. Let me stay the / growth of his beard, if thou delay me not the knowledge of his chin.
Well, God will send more if the man is grateful. I'll wait for his beard to grow, if you won't keep me waiting to know whose chin it is.
It is young Orlando, that tripped up the wrestler's heels and your / heart both in an instant.
It's young Orlando, who tripped up the wrestler's heels and your heart at the same moment.
Nay, but the devil take mocking! Speak sad brow and true maid.
No, the devil take your teasing! Speak seriously, on your honour.

Alas the day, what shall I do with my doublet and hose? What did he / when thou saw'st him? What said he? How looked he? Wherein went he? / What makes he here? Did he ask for me? Where remains he? How parted he / with thee? And when shalt thou see him again? Answer me in one word.

Oh no, what shall I do with my doublet and hose? What was he doing when you saw him? What did he say? How did he look? What was he wearing? What's he doing here? Did he ask about me? Where's he staying? How did he leave you? And when will you see him again? Answer me in one word.
You must borrow me Gargantua's mouth first. 'Tis a word too great for / any mouth of this age's size. To say ay and no to these particulars is / more than to answer in a catechism.
You'll have to lend me Gargantua's mouth first. It's a word too big for any mouth of today's size. To say yes and no to all these questions is more than answering the catechism.
But doth he know that I am in this forest and in man's apparel? Looks / he as freshly as he did the day he wrestled?
But does he know I'm in this forest, and dressed as a man? Does he look as fresh as he did on the day of the wrestling?
It is as easy to count atomies as to resolve the propositions of a / lover. But take a taste of my finding him, and relish it with good / observance. I found him under a tree, like a dropped acorn.
It's as easy to count specks of dust as to answer a lover's questions. But have a taste of how I found him, and enjoy it with close attention. I found him under a tree, like a fallen acorn.
It may well be called Jove's tree when it drops forth such fruit.
It may well be called Jove's tree, if it drops such fruit. (The oak was sacred to Jove.)
There lay he, stretched along like a wounded knight.
There he lay, stretched out like a wounded knight.
Though it be pity to see such a sight, it well becomes the ground.
Though it's a pity to see such a sight, it suits the ground well.
Cry "holla!" to thy tongue, I prithee. It curvets unseasonably. He was / furnished like a hunter.
Shout 'whoa!' to your tongue, please. It's prancing about at the wrong moments. He was dressed like a hunter.
O, ominous! He comes to kill my heart.
Oh, an omen! He's come to kill my heart (with a pun on hart, a deer).
I would sing my song without a burden. Thou bring'st me out of tune.
I'd like to sing my song without a chorus. You put me off the tune.
Do you not know I am a woman? When I think, I must speak. Sweet, say / on.
Don't you know I'm a woman? When I think, I have to speak. Sweetheart, go on.
You bring me out. Soft, comes he not here?
You put me off. Wait, isn't he coming this way?
'Tis he! Slink by, and note him.
It's him! Slip aside and watch him.
I thank you for your company but, good faith, I had as lief have been / myself alone.
Thank you for your company, but honestly, I'd just as soon have been on my own.
And so had I, but yet, for fashion sake, I thank you too for your / society.
And so would I; but still, for the sake of good manners, I thank you too for your company.
God be wi' you, let's meet as little as we can.
Goodbye, and let's meet as little as we can.
I do desire we may be better strangers.
I hope we can become even better strangers.
I pray you, mar no more trees with writing love songs in their barks.
Please don't spoil any more trees by writing love songs on their bark.
I pray you, mar no more of my verses with reading them ill-favouredly.
Please don't spoil any more of my verses by reading them so badly.
I do not like her name.
There was no thought of pleasing you when she was christened.
No one was thinking of pleasing you when she was christened.
Just as high as my heart.
Just as high as my heart.
You are full of pretty answers. Have you not been acquainted with / goldsmiths' wives, and conned them out of rings?
You're full of pretty answers. Haven't you been friendly with goldsmiths' wives, and learned them by heart from the mottoes in rings?
Not so; but I answer you right painted cloth, from whence you have / studied your questions.
No; I'm answering you in the style of the painted wall-hangings, where you learned your questions.
You have a nimble wit. I think 'twas made of Atalanta's heels. Will you / sit down with me? And we two will rail against our mistress the world / and all our misery.
You have a quick wit. I think it was made of Atalanta's heels. Will you sit down with me? We'll rant together against our mistress the world and all our misery.
I will chide no breather in the world but myself, against whom I know / most faults.
I won't criticise any living person in the world except myself, in whom I know most faults.
The worst fault you have is to be in love.
Your worst fault is being in love.
'Tis a fault I will not change for your best virtue. I am weary of you.
It's a fault I wouldn't swap for your best virtue. I'm tired of you.
By my troth, I was seeking for a fool when I found you.
Honestly, I was looking for a fool when I found you.
He is drowned in the brook. Look but in, and you shall see him.
He's drowned in the stream. Just look in, and you'll see him.
There I shall see mine own figure.
I'll see my own reflection there.
Which I take to be either a fool or a cipher.
Which I take to be either a fool or a zero.
I'll tarry no longer with you. Farewell, good Signior Love.
I won't stay with you any longer. Goodbye, good Signor Love.
I am glad of your departure. Adieu, good Monsieur Melancholy.
I'm glad you're going. Goodbye, good Monsieur Melancholy.
I will speak to him like a saucy lackey, and under that habit play the / knave with him. / Do you hear, forester?
I'll speak to him like a cheeky servant, and play tricks on him in that disguise. Do you hear, forester?
Very well. What do you want?
I pray you, what is't o'clock?
You should ask me what time o' day. There's no clock in the forest.
You should ask me what time of day it is. There's no clock in the forest.
Then there is no true lover in the forest, else sighing every minute / and groaning every hour would detect the lazy foot of time as well as a / clock.
Then there's no true lover in the forest; otherwise sighing every minute and groaning every hour would mark the lazy foot of time as well as a clock.
And why not the swift foot of time? Had not that been as proper?
And why not the swift foot of time? Wouldn't that have been just as right?
By no means, sir. Time travels in divers paces with divers persons. / I'll tell you who time ambles withal, who time trots withal, who time / gallops withal, and who he stands still withal.
Not at all, sir. Time travels at different speeds for different people. I'll tell you who time ambles with, who time trots with, who time gallops with, and who he stands still with.
I prithee, who doth he trot withal?
Please, who does he trot with?

Marry, he trots hard with a young maid between the contract of her / marriage and the day it is solemnized. If the interim be but a / se'nnight, time's pace is so hard that it seems the length of seven / year.
Well, he trots hard with a young woman between her engagement and her wedding day. Even if the gap is only a week, time goes so roughly that it seems to last seven years.

With a priest that lacks Latin and a rich man that hath not the gout; / for the one sleeps easily because he cannot study, and the other lives / merrily because he feels no pain; the one lacking the burden of lean / and wasteful learning, the other knowing no burden of heavy tedious / penury. These time ambles withal.

With a priest who has no Latin and a rich man who doesn't have gout. The one sleeps easily because he can't study, and the other lives merrily because he feels no pain; the one is spared the burden of dry, exhausting learning, the other knows nothing of the heavy, tedious burden of poverty. Time ambles with these.
With a thief to the gallows; for though he go as softly as foot can / fall, he thinks himself too soon there.
With a thief going to the gallows; because however slowly he walks, he thinks he gets there too soon.
Who does it stand still with?
With lawyers in the vacation; for they sleep between term and term, and / then they perceive not how time moves.
With lawyers in the holidays; because they sleep from one term to the next, so they don't notice time moving.
Where do you live, pretty youth?
With this shepherdess, my sister, here in the skirts of the forest, / like fringe upon a petticoat.
With this shepherdess, my sister, here on the edge of the forest, like a fringe on a petticoat.
Are you native of this place?
As the coney that you see dwell where she is kindled.
Like the rabbit you see living where she was born.
Your accent is something finer than you could purchase in so removed a / dwelling.
Your accent is rather more refined than you could pick up in such a remote place.

I have been told so of many. But indeed an old religious uncle of mine / taught me to speak, who was in his youth an inland man, one that knew / courtship too well, for there he fell in love. I have heard him read / many lectures against it, and I thank God I am not a woman, to be / touched with so many giddy offences as he hath generally taxed their / whole sex withal.

Many people have told me that. In fact an old uncle of mine, a religious man, taught me to speak. In his youth he lived in the town, and he knew courtship only too well, because that's where he fell in love. I've heard him give many lectures against love, and I thank God I'm not a woman, to be infected with all the giddy faults he blamed the whole female sex for.
Can you remember any of the principal evils that he laid to the charge / of women?
Can you remember any of the main evils he accused women of?
There were none principal. They were all like one another as halfpence / are, every one fault seeming monstrous till his fellow fault came to / match it.
There were no main ones. They were all as like one another as halfpennies; each fault seemed monstrous until the next fault came along to match it.
I prithee recount some of them.
Please tell me some of them.

No. I will not cast away my physic but on those that are sick. There is / a man haunts the forest that abuses our young plants with carving / "Rosalind" on their barks; hangs odes upon hawthorns and elegies on / brambles; all, forsooth, deifying the name of Rosalind. If I could meet / that fancy-monger, I would give him some good counsel, for he seems to / have the quotidian of love upon him.

No. I won't waste my medicine except on those who are sick. There's a man haunting the forest who damages our young trees by carving 'Rosalind' on their bark, hangs odes on hawthorns and laments on brambles, all, if you please, worshipping the name of Rosalind. If I could meet that dealer in fancies, I'd give him some good advice, because he seems to have the daily fever of love.
I am he that is so love-shaked. I pray you tell me your remedy.
I'm the one who's so shaken by love. Please tell me your cure.
There is none of my uncle's marks upon you. He taught me how to know a / man in love, in which cage of rushes I am sure you are not prisoner.
There's none of my uncle's signs on you. He taught me how to recognise a man in love, and I'm sure you're not a prisoner in that cage of rushes.

A lean cheek, which you have not; a blue eye and sunken, which you have / not; an unquestionable spirit, which you have not; a beard neglected, / which you have not—but I pardon you for that, for simply your having in / beard is a younger brother's revenue. Then your hose should be / ungartered, your bonnet unbanded, your sleeve unbuttoned, your shoe / untied, and everything about you demonstrating a careless desolation. / But you are no such man. You are rather point-device in your / accoutrements, as loving yourself than seeming the lover of any other.

A thin face, which you haven't got; dark-ringed, sunken eyes, which you haven't got; a moody spirit that won't talk, which you haven't got; an untrimmed beard, which you haven't got (but I forgive you for that, because what you have in the way of beard is as small as a younger brother's income). Then your stockings should be ungartered, your hat without its band, your sleeve unbuttoned, your shoe untied, and everything about you showing careless misery. But you're not that kind of man. You're more neat and precise in your dress, as if you loved yourself rather than looking like the lover of anyone else.
Fair youth, I would I could make thee believe I love.
Fair youth, I wish I could make you believe I'm in love.

Me believe it? You may as soon make her that you love believe it, which / I warrant she is apter to do than to confess she does. That is one of / the points in the which women still give the lie to their consciences. / But, in good sooth, are you he that hangs the verses on the trees, / wherein Rosalind is so admired?

Make me believe it? You might as well make the woman you love believe it, which I promise you she's more likely to do than to admit she does. That's one of the ways in which women always lie against their own consciences. But, honestly, are you the one who hangs the verses on the trees that praise Rosalind so much?
I swear to thee, youth, by the white hand of Rosalind, I am that he, / that unfortunate he.
I swear to you, youth, by Rosalind's white hand, I am the one, that unlucky one.
But are you so much in love as your rhymes speak?
But are you as much in love as your rhymes say?
Neither rhyme nor reason can express how much.
Neither rhyme nor reason can express how much.

Love is merely a madness, and, I tell you, deserves as well a dark / house and a whip as madmen do; and the reason why they are not so / punished and cured is that the lunacy is so ordinary that the whippers / are in love too. Yet I profess curing it by counsel.

Love is just a madness and, I tell you, deserves a dark room and a whip as much as madmen do. The reason lovers aren't punished and cured like that is that the madness is so common that the whippers are in love too. But I claim to cure it by advice.
Did you ever cure any so?
Did you ever cure anyone like that?

Yes, one, and in this manner. He was to imagine me his love, his / mistress, and I set him every day to woo me; at which time would I, / being but a moonish youth, grieve, be effeminate, changeable, longing / and liking, proud, fantastical, apish, shallow, inconstant, full of / tears, full of smiles; for every passion something and for no passion / truly anything, as boys and women are for the most part cattle of this / colour; would now like him, now loathe him; then entertain him, then / forswear him; now weep for him, then spit at him; that I drave my / suitor from his mad humour of love to a living humour of madness, which / was to forswear the full stream of the world and to live in a nook / merely monastic. And thus I cured him, and this way will I take upon me / to wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep's heart, that there shall / not be one spot of love in 't.

Yes, one, and this is how. He had to imagine I was his love, his mistress, and I made him come every day to woo me. And then I, being a moody youth, would grieve, be girlish, changeable, longing and liking, proud, full of whims, silly, shallow, fickle, full of tears, full of smiles; showing a bit of every emotion and truly feeling none, since boys and women are mostly creatures of this kind. I would like him one moment, loathe him the next; welcome him, then reject him; weep for him, then spit at him. So I drove my suitor from his mad mood of love into a real mood of madness, which was to give up the busy world altogether and live in a corner like a monk. That's how I cured him, and this is the way I'll undertake to wash your liver (the seat of love) as clean as a healthy sheep's heart, so that there won't be a single spot of love left in it.
I would not be cured, youth.
I don't want to be cured, youth.
I would cure you, if you would but call me Rosalind and come every day / to my cote and woo me.
I would cure you, if you would just call me Rosalind and come every day to my cottage and woo me.
Now, by the faith of my love, I will. Tell me where it is.
Now, by the truth of my love, I will. Tell me where it is.
Go with me to it, and I'll show it you; and by the way you shall tell / me where in the forest you live. Will you go?
Come with me and I'll show you, and on the way you can tell me where you live in the forest. Will you come?
With all my heart, good youth.
With all my heart, good youth.
Nay, you must call me Rosalind. Come, sister, will you go?
No, you must call me Rosalind. Come, sister, will you come?
Come apace, good Audrey. I will fetch up your goats, Audrey. And how, / Audrey? Am I the man yet? Doth my simple feature content you?
Hurry up, good Audrey. I'll round up your goats, Audrey. And how about it, Audrey? Am I the man for you yet? Do my plain features please you?
Your features, Lord warrant us! What features?
Your features, Lord help us! What features?
I am here with thee and thy goats, as the most capricious poet, honest / Ovid, was among the Goths.
I'm here with you and your goats, like the most capricious (goat-like) poet, honest Ovid, was among the Goths. (Ovid was exiled among the Getae; 'Goths' puns on goats.)
[Aside] O knowledge ill-inhabited, worse than Jove in a thatched / house!
Oh, learning badly housed, worse than Jove in a thatched cottage!

When a man's verses cannot be understood, nor a man's good wit seconded / with the forward child, understanding, it strikes a man more dead than / a great reckoning in a little room. Truly, I would the gods had made / thee poetical.

When a man's verses can't be understood, and a man's good wit isn't backed up by that precocious child, understanding, it strikes a man deader than a big bill in a small room. Truly, I wish the gods had made you poetical.
I do not know what "poetical" is. Is it honest in deed and word? Is it / a true thing?
I don't know what 'poetical' is. Is it honest in deed and word? Is it a true thing?
No, truly; for the truest poetry is the most feigning, and lovers are / given to poetry, and what they swear in poetry may be said, as lovers, / they do feign.
No, truly; because the truest poetry is the most made-up, and lovers love poetry, and what they swear in poetry, you could say, as lovers, they're making up.
Do you wish, then, that the gods had made me poetical?
Then do you wish the gods had made me poetical?
I do, truly, for thou swear'st to me thou art honest. Now if thou wert / a poet, I might have some hope thou didst feign.
I do, truly, because you swear to me you're chaste. Now if you were a poet, I might have some hope you were making it up.
Would you not have me honest?
Don't you want me to be chaste?
No, truly, unless thou wert hard-favoured; for honesty coupled to / beauty is to have honey a sauce to sugar.
No, truly, unless you were ugly; because chastity combined with beauty is like putting honey on sugar.
A fool full of good matter!
Well, I am not fair, and therefore I pray the gods make me honest.
Well, I'm not beautiful, so I pray the gods make me chaste.
Truly, and to cast away honesty upon a foul slut were to put good meat / into an unclean dish.
Truly, and to waste chastity on an ugly slut would be like putting good meat into a dirty dish.
I am not a slut, though I thank the gods I am foul.
I'm not a slut, though I thank the gods I'm ugly.

Well, praised be the gods for thy foulness; sluttishness may come / hereafter. But be it as it may be, I will marry thee. And to that end I / have been with Sir Oliver Martext, the vicar of the next village, who / hath promised to meet me in this place of the forest and to couple us.

Well, praise the gods for your ugliness; the sluttishness may come later. But however it may be, I'll marry you. And for that purpose I've been to Sir Oliver Martext, the vicar of the next village, who has promised to meet me here in the forest and marry us.
[Aside] I would fain see this meeting.
I'd love to see this meeting.
Well, the gods give us joy!
Well, the gods give us joy!

Amen. A man may, if he were of a fearful heart, stagger in this / attempt, for here we have no temple but the wood, no assembly but / horn-beasts. But what though? Courage! As horns are odious, they are / necessary. It is said, "Many a man knows no end of his goods." Right. / Many a man has good horns and knows no end of them. Well, that is the / dowry of his wife; 'tis none of his own getting. Horns? Even so. Poor / men alone? No, no, the noblest deer hath them as huge as the rascal. Is / the single man therefore blessed? No. As a walled town is more worthier / than a village, so is the forehead of a married man more honourable / than the bare brow of a bachelor. And by how much defence is better / than no skill, by so much is horn more precious than to want.

Amen. A man who was faint-hearted might falter at this, because here we have no church but the wood, no congregation but horned beasts. But so what? Courage! Horns are hateful, but they're unavoidable. People say, 'Many a man knows no end of his goods.' Right: many a man has good horns and knows no end of them. Well, that's his wife's dowry; he didn't get them himself. Horns? Just so. Only for poor men? No, no, the noblest deer has horns as huge as the scrawniest. So is the single man blessed? No. Just as a walled town is worthier than a village, so a married man's forehead is more honourable than a bachelor's bare brow. And as much as being able to defend yourself is better than having no skill, so much more precious is a horn than having none.
Here comes Sir Oliver. Sir Oliver Martext, you are well met. Will you / dispatch us here under this tree, or shall we go with you to your / chapel?
Here comes Sir Oliver. Sir Oliver Martext, good to see you. Will you get us married here under this tree, or shall we go with you to your chapel?
Is there none here to give the woman?
Is there no one here to give the woman away?
I will not take her on gift of any man.
I won't take her as a gift from any man.
Truly, she must be given, or the marriage is not lawful.
Truly, she has to be given away, or the marriage isn't lawful.
[Coming forward] Proceed, proceed. I'll give her.
Go on, go on. I'll give her away.
Good even, good Master What-ye-call't, how do you, sir? You are very / well met. God 'ild you for your last company. I am very glad to see / you. Even a toy in hand here, sir. Nay, pray be covered.

Good evening, good Master What's-your-name. How are you, sir? Very good to see you. God reward you for your company last time. I'm very glad to see you. Just a little business in hand here, sir. No, please, keep your hat on.
Do you want to be married, motley?
As the ox hath his bow, sir, the horse his curb, and the falcon her / bells, so man hath his desires; and as pigeons bill, so wedlock would / be nibbling.
As the ox has his yoke, sir, the horse his bit, and the falcon her bells, so man has his desires; and as pigeons bill and coo, so marriage wants to be nibbling.

And will you, being a man of your breeding, be married under a bush / like a beggar? Get you to church, and have a good priest that can tell / you what marriage is. This fellow will but join you together as they / join wainscot; then one of you will prove a shrunk panel, and like / green timber, warp, warp.

And will you, a man of your upbringing, get married under a bush like a beggar? Go to church, and have a good priest who can tell you what marriage is. This fellow will only join you together the way they join wood panelling; then one of you will turn out to be a shrunken panel and, like unseasoned timber, warp, warp.

[Aside] I am not in the mind but I were better to be married of him / than of another, for he is not like to marry me well, and not being / well married, it will be a good excuse for me hereafter to leave my / wife.

I rather think I'd be better off being married by him than by anyone else, because he's not likely to marry me properly, and if I'm not properly married, it'll be a good excuse for me to leave my wife later on.
Go thou with me, and let me counsel thee.
Come with me, and let me advise you.

Come, sweet Audrey. We must be married, or we must live in bawdry. / Farewell, good Master Oliver. Not / O sweet Oliver, / O brave Oliver, / Leave me not behind thee. / But / Wind away,— / Begone, I say, / I will not to wedding with thee.

Come, sweet Audrey. We must get married, or we'll have to live in sin. Goodbye, good Master Oliver. Not (he sings snatches of a ballad) 'Oh sweet Oliver, oh brave Oliver, don't leave me behind you,' but 'Go away, be off, I say, I won't come to my wedding with you.'
'Tis no matter. Ne'er a fantastical knave of them all shall flout me / out of my calling.
It doesn't matter. No crazy rascal among them will mock me out of my profession.
Never talk to me, I will weep.
Don't talk to me. I'm going to cry.
Do, I prithee, but yet have the grace to consider that tears do not / become a man.
Do, please; but have the decency to remember that tears don't suit a man.
But have I not cause to weep?
But haven't I reason to cry?
As good cause as one would desire; therefore weep.
As good a reason as anyone could want; so cry.
His very hair is of the dissembling colour.
Even his hair is the colour of a liar's.
Something browner than Judas's. Marry, his kisses are Judas's own / children.
A bit browner than Judas's. And his kisses are Judas's own children.
I' faith, his hair is of a good colour.
Honestly, his hair is a good colour.
An excellent colour. Your chestnut was ever the only colour.
An excellent colour. Chestnut was always the only colour.
And his kissing is as full of sanctity as the touch of holy bread.
And his kissing is as holy as touching the communion bread.
He hath bought a pair of cast lips of Diana. A nun of winter's / sisterhood kisses not more religiously; the very ice of chastity is in / them.
He's bought a pair of lips cast off by Diana. A nun of winter's sisterhood doesn't kiss more religiously; the very ice of chastity is in them.
But why did he swear he would come this morning, and comes not?
But why did he swear he'd come this morning, and he doesn't come?
Nay, certainly, there is no truth in him.
Well, there's certainly no truth in him.
Yes. I think he is not a pick-purse nor a horse-stealer, but for his / verity in love, I do think him as concave as a covered goblet or a / worm-eaten nut.
Yes. I don't think he's a pickpocket or a horse thief, but as for his truth in love, I think he's as hollow as an empty covered goblet or a worm-eaten nut.
Yes, when he is in, but I think he is not in.
Yes, when he's in love; but I don't think he's in.
You have heard him swear downright he was.
You heard him swear outright that he was.
"Was" is not "is". Besides, the oath of a lover is no stronger than the / word of a tapster. They are both the confirmer of false reckonings. He / attends here in the forest on the Duke your father.
'Was' isn't 'is'. Besides, a lover's oath is no stronger than a barman's word; they both swear to false bills. He's here in the forest, serving the Duke your father.

I met the Duke yesterday, and had much question with him. He asked me / of what parentage I was. I told him, of as good as he, so he laughed / and let me go. But what talk we of fathers when there is such a man as / Orlando?

I met the Duke yesterday and talked with him a lot. He asked me who my parents were. I told him, as good as his, so he laughed and let me go. But why are we talking about fathers when there's such a man as Orlando?

O, that's a brave man! He writes brave verses, speaks brave words, / swears brave oaths, and breaks them bravely, quite traverse, athwart / the heart of his lover, as a puny tilter, that spurs his horse but on / one side, breaks his staff like a noble goose. But all's brave that / youth mounts and folly guides. Who comes here?

Oh, he's a fine man! He writes fine verses, speaks fine words, swears fine oaths and breaks them finely, crosswise against his lover's heart, like a feeble jouster who spurs his horse on one side only and breaks his lance across his opponent like a noble goose. But everything's fine that youth rides and folly steers. Who's coming?
Mistress and master, you have oft enquired / After the shepherd that complained of love, / Who you saw sitting by me on the turf, / Praising the proud disdainful shepherdess / That was his mistress.
Mistress and master, you've often asked about the shepherd who complained of love, whom you saw sitting beside me on the grass, praising the proud, scornful shepherdess who was his love.
If you will see a pageant truly played / Between the pale complexion of true love / And the red glow of scorn and proud disdain, / Go hence a little, and I shall conduct you, / If you will mark it.
If you want to see a show truly acted between the pale face of true love and the red glow of scorn and proud disdain, come a little way from here and I'll take you, if you'd like to watch it.
O, come, let us remove. / The sight of lovers feedeth those in love. / Bring us to this sight, and you shall say / I'll prove a busy actor in their play.
Oh, come, let's go. The sight of lovers feeds those who are in love. Take us to see it, and you'll find I'll play a busy part in their play.

Sweet Phoebe, do not scorn me, do not, Phoebe. / Say that you love me not, but say not so / In bitterness. The common executioner, / Whose heart th' accustomed sight of death makes hard, / Falls not the axe upon the humbled neck / But first begs pardon. Will you sterner be / Than he that dies and lives by bloody drops?

Sweet Phoebe, don't scorn me, don't, Phoebe. Say you don't love me, but don't say it bitterly. Even the public executioner, whose heart is hardened by the familiar sight of death, doesn't bring the axe down on the bowed neck without first asking pardon. Will you be harder than a man who lives and dies by shedding blood?

I would not be thy executioner; / I fly thee, for I would not injure thee. / Thou tell'st me there is murder in mine eye. / 'Tis pretty, sure, and very probable / That eyes, that are the frail'st and softest things, / Who shut their coward gates on atomies, / Should be called tyrants, butchers, murderers. / Now I do frown on thee with all my heart, / And if mine eyes can wound, now let them kill thee. / Now counterfeit to swoon; why, now fall down; / Or if thou canst not, O, for shame, for shame, / Lie not, to say mine eyes are murderers. / Now show the wound mine eye hath made in thee. / Scratch thee but with a pin, and there remains / Some scar of it; lean upon a rush, / The cicatrice and capable impressure / Thy palm some moment keeps. But now mine eyes, / Which I have darted at thee, hurt thee not; / Nor I am sure there is not force in eyes / That can do hurt.

I don't want to be your executioner. I run from you because I don't want to hurt you. You tell me there's murder in my eye. That's charming, certainly, and very likely, that eyes, the frailest and softest things, which shut their cowardly gates against specks of dust, should be called tyrants, butchers, murderers! Now I'm frowning at you with all my heart, and if my eyes can wound, let them kill you now. Now pretend to faint; go on, fall down. Or if you can't, then for shame, for shame, don't lie and say my eyes are murderers. Now show me the wound my eye has made in you. Just scratch yourself with a pin, and there's some scar left; lean on a reed, and your palm keeps the mark and impression of it for a moment. But my eyes, which I've shot at you, haven't hurt you. And I'm sure there's no power in eyes that can hurt.
O dear Phoebe, / If ever—as that ever may be near— / You meet in some fresh cheek the power of fancy, / Then shall you know the wounds invisible / That love's keen arrows make.
Oh, dear Phoebe, if ever (and may that day be soon) you meet the power of love in some young face, then you'll know the invisible wounds that love's sharp arrows make.
But till that time / Come not thou near me. And when that time comes, / Afflict me with thy mocks, pity me not, / As till that time I shall not pity thee.
But until that time, don't come near me. And when that time comes, torment me with your mockery and don't pity me, just as until then I won't pity you.

[Advancing] And why, I pray you? Who might be your mother, / That you insult, exult, and all at once, / Over the wretched? What though you have no beauty— / As, by my faith, I see no more in you / Than without candle may go dark to bed— / Must you be therefore proud and pitiless? / Why, what means this? Why do you look on me? / I see no more in you than in the ordinary / Of nature's sale-work. 'Od's my little life, / I think she means to tangle my eyes too! / No, faith, proud mistress, hope not after it. / 'Tis not your inky brows, your black silk hair, / Your bugle eyeballs, nor your cheek of cream, / That can entame my spirits to your worship. / You foolish shepherd, wherefore do you follow her, / Like foggy south, puffing with wind and rain? / You are a thousand times a properer man / Than she a woman. 'Tis such fools as you / That makes the world full of ill-favoured children. / 'Tis not her glass but you that flatters her, / And out of you she sees herself more proper / Than any of her lineaments can show her. / But, mistress, know yourself; down on your knees, / And thank heaven, fasting, for a good man's love. / For I must tell you friendly in your ear, / Sell when you can; you are not for all markets. / Cry the man mercy, love him, take his offer; / Foul is most foul, being foul to be a scoffer. / So take her to thee, shepherd. Fare you well.

And why not, may I ask? Who was your mother, that you insult and gloat, both at once, over this poor wretch? So what if you have no beauty (and honestly, I see no more in you than could go to bed in the dark without a candle), must you be proud and pitiless because of it? Why, what's this? Why are you looking at me? I see nothing more in you than in nature's ordinary mass-produced goods. God save my little life, I think she means to trap my eyes too! No, really, proud mistress, don't hope for it. It's not your inky eyebrows, your black silky hair, your glassy black eyeballs or your creamy cheek that can tame my spirit into worshipping you. You foolish shepherd, why do you follow her, like the foggy south wind puffing out wind and rain? You're a thousand times better-looking as a man than she is as a woman. It's fools like you who fill the world with ugly children. It's not her mirror that flatters her, it's you, and in you she sees herself as better-looking than any of her features really show. But, mistress, know yourself. Get down on your knees and thank heaven, with fasting, for a good man's love. Because I must tell you, as a friend, in your ear: sell while you can; you won't suit every market. Beg the man's pardon, love him, take his offer. Ugliness is ugliest when it's scornful too. So take her, shepherd. Goodbye.
Sweet youth, I pray you chide a year together! / I had rather hear you chide than this man woo.
Sweet youth, please scold me for a whole year! I'd rather hear you scold than this man woo.

He's fall'n in love with your foulness, and she'll fall in love with my / anger. If it be so, as fast as she answers thee with frowning looks, / I'll sauce her with bitter words. Why look you so upon me?

He's fallen in love with her ugliness, and she's going to fall in love with my anger. If that's how it is, then as fast as she answers you with frowns, I'll season her with bitter words. Why are you looking at me like that?
For no ill will I bear you.
Not out of any ill will towards you.

I pray you do not fall in love with me, / For I am falser than vows made in wine. / Besides, I like you not. If you will know my house, / 'Tis at the tuft of olives here hard by. / Will you go, sister? Shepherd, ply her hard. / Come, sister. Shepherdess, look on him better, / And be not proud. Though all the world could see, / None could be so abused in sight as he. / Come, to our flock.

Please don't fall in love with me, because I'm falser than vows made when drunk. Besides, I don't like you. If you want to know where I live, it's by the clump of olive trees close by here. Are you coming, sister? Shepherd, press her hard. Come, sister. Shepherdess, look on him more kindly, and don't be proud. Even if the whole world could see you, no one could be as deceived in what he sees as he is. Come, back to our flock.
Dead shepherd, now I find thy saw of might: / "Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?"
Dead shepherd, now I understand the power of your saying: 'Whoever loved that didn't love at first sight?' (A line from Marlowe's poem Hero and Leander.)
Ha, what are you saying, Silvius?
Why, I am sorry for thee, gentle Silvius.
Why, I'm sorry for you, gentle Silvius.
Wherever sorrow is, relief would be. / If you do sorrow at my grief in love, / By giving love your sorrow and my grief / Were both extermined.
Wherever there's sorrow, there should be relief. If you're sorry for my grief in love, then by giving me your love, both your sorrow and my grief would be wiped out.
Thou hast my love. Is not that neighbourly?
You have my love, as a neighbour. Isn't that neighbourly?

Why, that were covetousness. / Silvius, the time was that I hated thee; / And yet it is not that I bear thee love; / But since that thou canst talk of love so well, / Thy company, which erst was irksome to me, / I will endure, and I'll employ thee too. / But do not look for further recompense / Than thine own gladness that thou art employed.

Why, that would be greed. Silvius, there was a time when I hated you. And it's not that I love you now; but since you can talk about love so well, I'll put up with your company, which used to annoy me, and I'll give you a job too. But don't expect any other reward than your own pleasure at being employed.

So holy and so perfect is my love, / And I in such a poverty of grace, / That I shall think it a most plenteous crop / To glean the broken ears after the man / That the main harvest reaps. Loose now and then / A scattered smile, and that I'll live upon.

My love is so holy and so perfect, and I'm so poor in your favour, that I'll think it a rich harvest just to pick up the broken ears of corn left behind by the man who reaps the main crop. Let fall a stray smile now and then, and I'll live on that.
Know'st thou the youth that spoke to me erewhile?
Do you know the young man who spoke to me just now?
Not very well, but I have met him oft, / And he hath bought the cottage and the bounds / That the old carlot once was master of.
Not very well, but I've met him often. He's bought the cottage and the land that the old peasant used to own.

Think not I love him, though I ask for him. / 'Tis but a peevish boy—yet he talks well. / But what care I for words? Yet words do well / When he that speaks them pleases those that hear. / It is a pretty youth—not very pretty— / But sure he's proud, and yet his pride becomes him. / He'll make a proper man. The best thing in him / Is his complexion; and faster than his tongue / Did make offence, his eye did heal it up. / He is not very tall, yet for his years he's tall; / His leg is but so-so, and yet 'tis well. / There was a pretty redness in his lip, / A little riper and more lusty red / Than that mixed in his cheek. 'Twas just the difference / Betwixt the constant red and mingled damask. / There be some women, Silvius, had they marked him / In parcels as I did, would have gone near / To fall in love with him; but for my part / I love him not nor hate him not; and yet / I have more cause to hate him than to love him. / For what had he to do to chide at me? / He said mine eyes were black and my hair black, / And now I am remembered, scorned at me. / I marvel why I answered not again. / But that's all one: omittance is no quittance. / I'll write to him a very taunting letter, / And thou shalt bear it. Wilt thou, Silvius?

Don't think I love him, though I ask about him. He's only a bad-tempered boy; still, he talks well. But what do I care about words? Yet words work well when the speaker pleases the people who hear them. He's a pretty youth; not very pretty; but he's certainly proud, and yet his pride suits him. He'll make a fine man. The best thing about him is his complexion; and faster than his tongue gave offence, his eye healed it. He's not very tall, but he's tall for his age. His leg is only so-so, and yet it's nice. There was a pretty redness in his lip, a little riper and a deeper red than the colour mixed in his cheek: just the difference between plain red and a pink-and-white damask rose. There are some women, Silvius, who, if they'd studied him piece by piece as I did, would have come close to falling in love with him. But as for me, I don't love him or hate him; and yet I have more reason to hate him than love him. Because what business did he have scolding me? He said my eyes were black and my hair was black, and, now I come to think of it, he mocked me. I wonder why I didn't answer him back. But it makes no difference: not paying a debt now doesn't cancel it. I'll write him a very taunting letter, and you'll deliver it. Will you, Silvius?
I'll write it straight, / The matter's in my head and in my heart. / I will be bitter with him and passing short. / Go with me, Silvius.
I'll write it at once. What I want to say is in my head and in my heart. I'll be bitter with him and very short. Come with me, Silvius.
I prithee, pretty youth, let me be better acquainted with thee.
Please, pretty youth, let me get to know you better.
They say you are a melancholy fellow.
They say you're a melancholy fellow.
I am so; I do love it better than laughing.
I am. I like it better than laughing.
Those that are in extremity of either are abominable fellows, and / betray themselves to every modern censure worse than drunkards.
Those who go to extremes either way are horrible people, and lay themselves open to every common criticism worse than drunkards do.
Why, 'tis good to be sad and say nothing.
Why, it's good to be sad and say nothing.
Why then, 'tis good to be a post.
Why then, it's good to be a post.

I have neither the scholar's melancholy, which is emulation; nor the / musician's, which is fantastical; nor the courtier's, which is proud; / nor the soldier's, which is ambitious; nor the lawyer's, which is / politic; nor the lady's, which is nice; nor the lover's, which is all / these; but it is a melancholy of mine own, compounded of many simples, / extracted from many objects, and indeed the sundry contemplation of my / travels, in which my often rumination wraps me in a most humorous / sadness.

I haven't got the scholar's melancholy, which is envy; or the musician's, which is fanciful; or the courtier's, which is proud; or the soldier's, which is ambitious; or the lawyer's, which is scheming; or the lady's, which is fussy; or the lover's, which is all of these. It's a melancholy of my own, mixed from many ingredients, drawn from many things, and in fact from the various thoughts of my travels, and when I brood on them often they wrap me in a most moody sadness.
A traveller! By my faith, you have great reason to be sad. I fear you / have sold your own lands to see other men's. Then to have seen much and / to have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands.
A traveller! Honestly, you have good reason to be sad. I'm afraid you've sold your own lands to see other men's. And to have seen a lot and have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands.
Yes, I have gained my experience.
And your experience makes you sad. I had rather have a fool to make me / merry than experience to make me sad—and to travel for it too.
And your experience makes you sad. I'd rather have a fool to make me merry than experience to make me sad; and to travel for it too!
Good day and happiness, dear Rosalind!
Good day and happiness, dear Rosalind!
Nay, then, God be wi' you, an you talk in blank verse.
Well then, goodbye, if you're going to talk in blank verse.

Farewell, Monsieur Traveller. Look you lisp and wear strange suits; / disable all the benefits of your own country; be out of love with your / nativity, and almost chide God for making you that countenance you are, / or I will scarce think you have swam in a gondola.

Goodbye, Monsieur Traveller. Make sure you speak with an affected accent and wear foreign clothes; run down everything good about your own country; fall out of love with where you were born, and almost scold God for giving you the face you've got; or else I'll hardly believe you've ever been in a gondola.
Why, how now, Orlando, where have you been all this while? You a lover! / An you serve me such another trick, never come in my sight more.
Well now, Orlando, where have you been all this time? You, a lover! If you play another trick like that on me, never come near me again.
My fair Rosalind, I come within an hour of my promise.
My fair Rosalind, I've come within an hour of the time I promised.

Break an hour's promise in love? He that will divide a minute into a / thousand parts, and break but a part of the thousand part of a minute / in the affairs of love, it may be said of him that Cupid hath clapped / him o' the shoulder, but I'll warrant him heart-whole.

Break a promise in love by an hour? Someone who would divide a minute into a thousand parts and be late by even part of a thousandth of a minute in matters of love, you could say Cupid has tapped him on the shoulder, but I'll bet his heart is untouched.
Nay, an you be so tardy, come no more in my sight. I had as lief be / wooed of a snail.
No, if you're going to be so late, don't come near me again. I'd just as soon be wooed by a snail.
Ay, of a snail, for though he comes slowly, he carries his house on his / head—a better jointure, I think, than you make a woman. Besides, he / brings his destiny with him.
Yes, by a snail; because though he comes slowly, he carries his house on his head, a better marriage settlement, I think, than you can give a woman. Besides, he brings his destiny with him.
Why, horns, which such as you are fain to be beholding to your wives / for. But he comes armed in his fortune and prevents the slander of his / wife.
Why, horns, which men like you have to thank your wives for. But he comes already armed with his fate, and so heads off any gossip about his wife.
Virtue is no horn-maker and my Rosalind is virtuous.
Virtue doesn't make horns, and my Rosalind is virtuous.
It pleases him to call you so, but he hath a Rosalind of a better leer / than you.
He likes to call you that, but he has a Rosalind with a better face than you.
Come, woo me, woo me, for now I am in a holiday humour, and like enough / to consent. What would you say to me now, an I were your very, very / Rosalind?
Come on, woo me, woo me, because I'm in a holiday mood now and quite likely to say yes. What would you say to me now, if I were your very, very Rosalind?
I would kiss before I spoke.

Nay, you were better speak first, and when you were gravelled for lack / of matter, you might take occasion to kiss. Very good orators, when / they are out, they will spit; and for lovers lacking—God warn / us—matter, the cleanliest shift is to kiss.

No, you'd better speak first, and when you were stuck for something to say, you could take the chance to kiss. Very good speakers, when they forget their lines, spit; and for lovers lacking (God help us) something to say, the neatest way out is to kiss.
How if the kiss be denied?
What if the kiss is refused?
Then she puts you to entreaty, and there begins new matter.
Then she makes you beg, and that gives you something new to say.
Who could be out, being before his beloved mistress?
Who could be stuck for words, standing in front of the mistress he loves?
Marry, that should you, if I were your mistress, or I should think my / honesty ranker than my wit.
Why, you would, if I were your mistress; otherwise I'd think my virtue was looser than my wit.
What, put out of my suit? (Stuck in my wooing.)
Not out of your apparel, and yet out of your suit. Am not I your / Rosalind?
Not out of your clothes, and yet out of your suit. Aren't I your Rosalind?
I take some joy to say you are because I would be talking of her.
I'm happy to say you are, because I'd like to be talking about her.
Well, in her person, I say I will not have you.
Well, speaking as her, I say I won't have you.
Then, in mine own person, I die.
Then, speaking as myself, I'll die.

No, faith, die by attorney. The poor world is almost six thousand years / old, and in all this time there was not any man died in his own person, / videlicet, in a love-cause. Troilus had his brains dashed out with a / Grecian club, yet he did what he could to die before, and he is one of / the patterns of love.
