Leander, he would have lived many a fair year / though Hero had turned nun, if it had not been for a hot midsummer / night; for, good youth, he went but forth to wash him in the Hellespont / and, being taken with the cramp, was drowned; and the foolish / chroniclers of that age found it was Hero of Sestos. But these are all / lies. Men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but / not for love.

No, really, die by proxy. The poor world is almost six thousand years old, and in all that time no man has ever died himself, that is to say, for love. Troilus had his brains smashed out with a Greek club, yet he did all he could to die of love before that, and he's one of the great models of love. Leander would have lived many a good year, even if Hero had become a nun, if it hadn't been for a hot midsummer night. Because, good youth, he only went out to wash in the Hellespont, got cramp and was drowned, and the foolish historians of that time decided it was because of Hero of Sestos. But these are all lies. Men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but not for love.
I would not have my right Rosalind of this mind, for I protest her / frown might kill me.
I wouldn't want my real Rosalind to think like that, because I swear her frown could kill me.
By this hand, it will not kill a fly. But come, now I will be your / Rosalind in a more coming-on disposition, and ask me what you will, I / will grant it.
I swear by this hand, it wouldn't kill a fly. But come on, now I'll be your Rosalind in a more encouraging mood. Ask me whatever you like, and I'll grant it.
Yes, faith, will I, Fridays and Saturdays and all.
Yes, really, I will, Fridays and Saturdays and all.
Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing?—Come, sister, you / shall be the priest and marry us.—Give me your hand, Orlando.—What do / you say, sister?
Well then, can you have too much of a good thing? Come, sister, you shall be the priest and marry us. Give me your hand, Orlando. What do you say, sister?
You have to begin, 'Will you, Orlando...'
Go to.—Will you, Orlando, have to wife this Rosalind?
All right. Will you, Orlando, take this Rosalind as your wife?
Why now, as fast as she can marry us.
Why, now, as fast as she can marry us.
Then you must say "I take thee, Rosalind, for wife."
Then you must say, 'I take you, Rosalind, as my wife.'
I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.
I take you, Rosalind, as my wife.
I might ask you for your commission. But I do take thee, Orlando, for / my husband. There's a girl goes before the priest, and certainly a / woman's thought runs before her actions.
I could ask you what authority you have. But I do take you, Orlando, as my husband. There's a girl who runs ahead of the priest; and certainly a woman's thoughts run ahead of her actions.
So do all thoughts. They are winged.
So do all thoughts. They have wings.
Now tell me how long you would have her after you have possessed her.
Now tell me how long you would keep her after you've won her.

Say "a day" without the "ever." No, no, Orlando, men are April when / they woo, December when they wed. Maids are May when they are maids, / but the sky changes when they are wives. I will be more jealous of thee / than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen, more clamorous than a parrot / against rain, more new-fangled than an ape, more giddy in my desires / than a monkey. I will weep for nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and / I will do that when you are disposed to be merry. I will laugh like a / hyena, and that when thou are inclined to sleep.

Say 'a day', without the 'ever'. No, no, Orlando: men are April when they woo and December when they marry. Girls are May while they're single, but the weather changes when they become wives. I'll be more jealous of you than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen, noisier than a parrot before rain, more taken with novelties than an ape, more giddy in my desires than a monkey. I'll cry over nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and I'll do it when you feel like being merry. I'll laugh like a hyena, and that'll be when you want to sleep.
But will my Rosalind do so?
But will my Rosalind do that?
By my life, she will do as I do.
On my life, she'll do as I do.

Or else she could not have the wit to do this. The wiser, the / waywarder. Make the doors upon a woman's wit, and it will out at the / casement. Shut that, and 'twill out at the keyhole. Stop that, 'twill / fly with the smoke out at the chimney.

Otherwise she wouldn't have the wit to do it. The wiser, the more wayward. Shut the doors on a woman's wit, and it'll get out through the window. Shut that, and it'll get out through the keyhole. Block that, and it'll fly out with the smoke up the chimney.
A man that had a wife with such a wit, he might say, "Wit, whither / wilt?"
A man with a wife with a wit like that might say, 'Wit, where are you off to?'
Nay, you might keep that check for it till you met your wife's wit / going to your neighbour's bed.
No, you could save that rebuke until you met your wife's wit heading for your neighbour's bed.
And what wit could wit have to excuse that?
And what wit could her wit have to excuse that?

Marry, to say she came to seek you there. You shall never take her / without her answer unless you take her without her tongue. O, that / woman that cannot make her fault her husband's occasion, let her never / nurse her child herself, for she will breed it like a fool.

Why, to say she went there to look for you. You'll never catch her without an answer, unless you catch her without her tongue. Oh, a woman who can't turn her own fault into her husband's, let her never nurse her own child, because she'll bring it up a fool.
For these two hours, Rosalind, I will leave thee.
For these two hours, Rosalind, I'll leave you.
Alas, dear love, I cannot lack thee two hours.
Oh, dear love, I can't do without you for two hours.
I must attend the Duke at dinner. By two o'clock I will be with thee / again.
I have to wait on the Duke at dinner. By two o'clock I'll be with you again.

Ay, go your ways, go your ways. I knew what you would prove. My friends / told me as much, and I thought no less. That flattering tongue of yours / won me. 'Tis but one cast away, and so, come death! Two o'clock is your / hour?

Yes, off you go, off you go. I knew how you'd turn out. My friends told me as much, and I thought so too. That flattering tongue of yours won me. It's just one more girl thrown away, and so, come death! Two o'clock is your time?

By my troth, and in good earnest, and so God mend me, and by all pretty / oaths that are not dangerous, if you break one jot of your promise or / come one minute behind your hour, I will think you the most pathetical / break-promise, and the most hollow lover, and the most unworthy of her / you call Rosalind that may be chosen out of the gross band of the / unfaithful. Therefore beware my censure, and keep your promise.

Truly, and in all seriousness, and so help me God, and by all the pretty oaths that aren't dangerous, if you break the smallest part of your promise or come one minute after your time, I'll think you the most miserable promise-breaker, the emptiest lover and the least worthy of the woman you call Rosalind that could be picked out of the whole huge crowd of the unfaithful. So beware of my judgment, and keep your promise.
With no less religion than if thou wert indeed my Rosalind. So, adieu.
As faithfully as if you really were my Rosalind. So, goodbye.
Well, Time is the old justice that examines all such offenders, and let / time try. Adieu.
Well, Time is the old judge who examines all such offenders, so let time decide. Goodbye.
You have simply misused our sex in your love-prate! We must have your / doublet and hose plucked over your head and show the world what the / bird hath done to her own nest.
You've completely slandered our sex in your love-chatter! We should pull your doublet and hose up over your head and show the world what the bird has done to her own nest.
O coz, coz, coz, my pretty little coz, that thou didst know how many / fathom deep I am in love! But it cannot be sounded; my affection hath / an unknown bottom, like the Bay of Portugal.
Oh, cousin, cousin, cousin, my pretty little cousin, if only you knew how many fathoms deep I am in love! But it can't be measured. My love has no known bottom, like the Bay of Portugal.
Or rather, bottomless, that as fast as you pour affection in, it runs / out.
Or rather it's bottomless, so that as fast as you pour love in, it runs out.

No, that same wicked bastard of Venus, that was begot of thought, / conceived of spleen, and born of madness, that blind rascally boy that / abuses everyone's eyes because his own are out, let him be judge how / deep I am in love. I'll tell thee, Aliena, I cannot be out of the sight / of Orlando. I'll go find a shadow and sigh till he come.

No, let that wicked bastard of Venus, who was fathered by fancy, conceived in impulse and born of madness, that blind rascal of a boy who deceives everyone's eyes because his own are gone, let him judge how deep I am in love. I tell you, Aliena, I can't bear to be out of Orlando's sight. I'll go and find some shade and sigh until he comes.
Which is he that killed the deer?
Which of you killed the deer?
Let's present him to the Duke, like a Roman conqueror, and it would do / well to set the deer's horns upon his head for a branch of victory. / Have you no song, forester, for this purpose?
Let's present him to the Duke like a Roman conqueror. It would be good to put the deer's horns on his head as a victory wreath. Have you got a song for the occasion, forester?
Sing it. 'Tis no matter how it be in tune, so it make noise enough.
Sing it. It doesn't matter if it's in tune, as long as it makes enough noise.

[Sings] / What shall he have that killed the deer? / His leather skin and horns to wear. / Then sing him home: / [The rest shall bear this burden] / Take thou no scorn to wear the horn. / It was a crest ere thou wast born. / Thy father's father wore it / And thy father bore it. / The horn, the horn, the lusty horn / Is not a thing to laugh to scorn.

What shall the man who killed the deer have? Its leather skin and horns to wear. Then sing him home. Don't be ashamed to wear the horn; it was a family crest before you were born. Your father's father wore it, and your father wore it too. The horn, the horn, the lusty horn, is nothing to laugh at.
How say you now? Is it not past two o'clock? And here much Orlando.
What do you say now? Isn't it past two o'clock? And not much sign of Orlando.
I warrant you, with pure love and troubled brain he hath ta'en his bow / and arrows and is gone forth to sleep.
I'll bet you, with pure love and a troubled mind, he's taken his bow and arrows and gone off to sleep.
My errand is to you, fair youth. / My gentle Phoebe did bid me give you this.
My errand is to you, fair youth. My gentle Phoebe told me to give you this.

I know not the contents, but, as I guess / By the stern brow and waspish action / Which she did use as she was writing of it, / It bears an angry tenor. Pardon me, / I am but as a guiltless messenger.
I don't know what's in it, but judging by the stern frown and angry gestures she made while she was writing it, it's an angry letter. Forgive me; I'm only the innocent messenger.

Patience herself would startle at this letter / And play the swaggerer. Bear this, bear all! / She says I am not fair, that I lack manners; / She calls me proud, and that she could not love me, / Were man as rare as phoenix. 'Od's my will, / Her love is not the hare that I do hunt. / Why writes she so to me? Well, shepherd, well, / This is a letter of your own device.

Patience herself would be startled by this letter and start swaggering. Put up with this and you'd put up with anything! She says I'm not good-looking, that I lack manners; she calls me proud, and says she couldn't love me even if men were as rare as the phoenix. God's will, her love isn't the game I'm hunting. Why does she write to me like this? Well, shepherd, well, you made this letter up yourself.
No, I protest, I know not the contents. / Phoebe did write it.
No, I swear, I don't know what's in it. Phoebe wrote it.

Come, come, you are a fool, / And turned into the extremity of love. / I saw her hand. She has a leathern hand, / A freestone-coloured hand. I verily did think / That her old gloves were on, but 'twas her hands. / She has a huswife's hand—but that's no matter. / I say she never did invent this letter; / This is a man's invention, and his hand.

Come on, you're a fool, driven to the extremes of love. I've seen her hand. She has a leathery hand, a sandstone-coloured hand. I really thought she had her old gloves on, but it was her hands. She has a housewife's hand; but that doesn't matter. I tell you she never made up this letter. This is a man's invention, and a man's handwriting.

Why, 'tis a boisterous and a cruel style, / A style for challengers. Why, she defies me, / Like Turk to Christian. Women's gentle brain / Could not drop forth such giant-rude invention, / Such Ethiop words, blacker in their effect / Than in their countenance. Will you hear the letter?

Why, it's a rough and cruel style, a style for someone challenging you to a duel. Why, she defies me like a Turk defying a Christian. A woman's gentle brain couldn't produce such giant-sized rudeness, such black words, blacker in what they mean than how they look. Do you want to hear the letter?
So please you, for I never heard it yet, / Yet heard too much of Phoebe's cruelty.
If you please, because I've never heard it, though I've heard too much of Phoebe's cruelty.
She Phoebes me. Mark how the tyrant writes. / [Reads] / Art thou god to shepherd turned, / That a maiden's heart hath burned? / Can a woman rail thus?

She Phoebes me: she's treating me the way she treats you. Listen to how the tyrant writes. 'Are you a god turned into a shepherd, that you have set a young girl's heart on fire?' Can a woman insult like that?

Why, thy godhead laid apart, / Warr'st thou with a woman's heart? / Did you ever hear such railing? / Whiles the eye of man did woo me, / That could do no vengeance to me. / Meaning me a beast. / If the scorn of your bright eyne / Have power to raise such love in mine, / Alack, in me what strange effect / Would they work in mild aspect? / Whiles you chid me, I did love, / How then might your prayers move? / He that brings this love to thee / Little knows this love in me; / And by him seal up thy mind, / Whether that thy youth and kind / Will the faithful offer take / Of me, and all that I can make, / Or else by him my love deny, / And then I'll study how to die.

'Why, putting your godhood aside, do you make war on a woman's heart?' Did you ever hear such insults? 'While men's eyes wooed me, they could do me no harm.' Meaning I'm an animal. 'If the scorn of your bright eyes has the power to stir such love in me, oh, what strange effect would they have on me if they looked kindly? While you scolded me, I loved you; then how might your pleas move me?' 'The man who brings this love to you knows little of this love in me. Seal up your answer and send it by him: whether your youth and nature will accept the faithful offer of me and all I have, or else refuse my love through him, and then I'll work out how to die.'

Do you pity him? No, he deserves no pity.—Wilt thou love such a woman? / What, to make thee an instrument and play false strains upon thee? Not / to be endured! Well, go your way to her, for I see love hath made thee / a tame snake, and say this to her: that if she love me, I charge her to / love thee; if she will not, I will never have her unless thou entreat / for her. If you be a true lover, hence, and not a word, for here comes / more company.

Do you pity him? No, he deserves no pity. Would you love a woman like that? What, to use you as an instrument and play false tunes on you? Not to be put up with! Well, go back to her, since I see love has made you a tame snake, and tell her this: that if she loves me, I order her to love you; if she won't, I'll never have her unless you plead for her. If you're a true lover, go, and not a word, because here comes more company.
Good morrow, fair ones. Pray you, if you know, / Where in the purlieus of this forest stands / A sheepcote fenced about with olive trees?
Good morning, fair ones. Please, if you know, where on the edge of this forest is there a sheepfold surrounded by olive trees?

West of this place, down in the neighbour bottom; / The rank of osiers, by the murmuring stream, / Left on your right hand, brings you to the place. / But at this hour the house doth keep itself. / There's none within.

West of here, down in the valley nearby. Keep the row of willows by the murmuring stream on your right, and it will bring you to the place. But at this hour the house is looking after itself. There's no one in.

If that an eye may profit by a tongue, / Then should I know you by description, / Such garments, and such years. "The boy is fair, / Of female favour, and bestows himself / Like a ripe sister; the woman low, / And browner than her brother." Are not you / The owner of the house I did inquire for?

If an eye can learn from a tongue, then I should know you from the description: such clothes, and such ages. 'The boy is fair, with a girl's face, and carries himself like a grown-up sister; the woman is short, and browner than her brother.' Aren't you the owners of the house I was asking about?
It is no boast, being asked, to say we are.
Since you ask, it's no boast to say we are.
Orlando doth commend him to you both, / And to that youth he calls his Rosalind / He sends this bloody napkin. Are you he?
Orlando sends his regards to you both, and to the youth he calls his Rosalind he sends this bloodstained handkerchief. Are you him?
I am. What must we understand by this?
I am. What are we to make of this?
Some of my shame, if you will know of me / What man I am, and how, and why, and where / This handkerchief was stained.
Something of my own shame, if you want to know from me what kind of man I am, and how, and why, and where this handkerchief was stained.

When last the young Orlando parted from you, / He left a promise to return again / Within an hour, and pacing through the forest, / Chewing the food of sweet and bitter fancy, / Lo, what befell. He threw his eye aside, / And mark what object did present itself. / Under an oak, whose boughs were mossed with age / And high top bald with dry antiquity, / A wretched ragged man, o'ergrown with hair, / Lay sleeping on his back; about his neck / A green and gilded snake had wreathed itself, / Who with her head, nimble in threats, approached / The opening of his mouth. But suddenly, / Seeing Orlando, it unlinked itself / And with indented glides did slip away / Into a bush; under which bush's shade / A lioness, with udders all drawn dry, / Lay couching, head on ground, with catlike watch / When that the sleeping man should stir. For 'tis / The royal disposition of that beast / To prey on nothing that doth seem as dead. / This seen, Orlando did approach the man / And found it was his brother, his elder brother.

When young Orlando last left you, he promised to come back within an hour. As he walked through the forest, chewing over his sweet and bitter thoughts of love, look what happened. He glanced to one side, and see what met his eye. Under an oak, whose branches were mossy with age and whose high top was bare with dry old age, a wretched, ragged man, overgrown with hair, lay asleep on his back. A green and gold snake had wound itself round his neck, and with its head, quick to threaten, it was moving towards his open mouth. But suddenly, seeing Orlando, it uncoiled itself and slid away in zigzag glides into a bush. In the shade of that bush a lioness, her udders sucked dry, lay crouching with her head on the ground, watching like a cat for the sleeping man to stir; because it's the royal nature of that beast not to prey on anything that seems dead. Seeing this, Orlando went up to the man, and found it was his brother, his elder brother.
O, I have heard him speak of that same brother, / And he did render him the most unnatural / That lived amongst men.
Oh, I've heard him speak of that same brother, and he described him as the most unnatural man alive.
And well he might so do, / For well I know he was unnatural.
And he was right to, because I know very well he was unnatural.
But, to Orlando: did he leave him there, / Food to the sucked and hungry lioness?
But, about Orlando: did he leave him there, as food for the hungry lioness with her sucked-dry udders?

Twice did he turn his back and purposed so; / But kindness, nobler ever than revenge, / And nature, stronger than his just occasion, / Made him give battle to the lioness, / Who quickly fell before him; in which hurtling / From miserable slumber I awaked.

Twice he turned his back, meaning to; but kindness, always nobler than revenge, and brotherly feeling, stronger than his good reason, made him fight the lioness, who quickly fell in front of him. In the noise of the struggle I woke from my wretched sleep.
Was't you that did so oft contrive to kill him?
Was it you who plotted so often to kill him?
'Twas I; but 'tis not I. I do not shame / To tell you what I was, since my conversion / So sweetly tastes, being the thing I am.
It was me; but it isn't me now. I'm not ashamed to tell you what I was, because my conversion tastes so sweet, now that I'm the man I am.
But what about the bloody handkerchief?

By and by. / When from the first to last betwixt us two / Tears our recountments had most kindly bathed— / As how I came into that desert place— / In brief, he led me to the gentle Duke, / Who gave me fresh array and entertainment, / Committing me unto my brother's love, / Who led me instantly unto his cave, / There stripped himself, and here upon his arm / The lioness had torn some flesh away, / Which all this while had bled; and now he fainted, / And cried in fainting upon Rosalind. / Brief, I recovered him, bound up his wound, / And after some small space, being strong at heart, / He sent me hither, stranger as I am, / To tell this story, that you might excuse / His broken promise, and to give this napkin, / Dyed in his blood, unto the shepherd youth / That he in sport doth call his Rosalind.

In a moment. When we'd told each other everything from first to last, with plenty of loving tears (including how I came to that wild place), in short, he took me to the gentle Duke, who gave me fresh clothes and food and put me in my brother's care. My brother took me straight to his cave and there took off his clothes, and here on his arm the lioness had torn away some flesh, which had been bleeding all this time. And then he fainted, and as he fainted he cried out for Rosalind. In short, I brought him round and bandaged his wound, and after a little while, his heart being strong, he sent me here, stranger though I am, to tell you this story, so that you'd forgive his broken promise, and to give this handkerchief, stained with his blood, to the young shepherd he calls his Rosalind in fun.
Why, how now, Ganymede, sweet Ganymede!
Many will swoon when they do look on blood.
Many people faint when they see blood.
There is more in it. Cousin—Ganymede!
There's more to it than that. Cousin! Ganymede!
I would I were at home.
I wish I were at home.
We'll lead you thither. / I pray you, will you take him by the arm?
We'll take you there. Please, will you take him by the arm?
Be of good cheer, youth. You a man? You lack a man's heart.
Cheer up, youth. You, a man? You haven't got a man's heart.
I do so, I confess it. Ah, sirrah, a body would think this was well / counterfeited. I pray you tell your brother how well I counterfeited. / Heigh-ho.
I haven't, I confess it. Ah, sir, anyone would think that was well faked. Please tell your brother how well I faked it. Heigh-ho.
This was not counterfeit. There is too great testimony in your / complexion that it was a passion of earnest.
That wasn't faked. Your complexion gives too much evidence that it was real emotion.
Well then, take a good heart, and counterfeit to be a man.
Well then, take heart, and fake being a man.
So I do. But, i' faith, I should have been a woman by right.
I'm doing that. But really, I should have been a woman by rights.
Come, you look paler and paler. Pray you draw homewards. Good sir, go / with us.
Come on, you're looking paler and paler. Please, let's head home. Good sir, come with us.
That will I, for I must bear answer back / How you excuse my brother, Rosalind.
I will, because I have to take back an answer about how you excuse my brother, Rosalind.
I shall devise something. But I pray you commend my counterfeiting to / him. Will you go?
I'll think of something. But please tell him how well I faked it. Shall we go?
We shall find a time, Audrey; patience, gentle Audrey.
We'll find a time, Audrey. Be patient, gentle Audrey.
Faith, the priest was good enough, for all the old gentleman's saying.
Honestly, the priest was good enough, whatever the old gentleman said.
A most wicked Sir Oliver, Audrey, a most vile Martext. But Audrey, / there is a youth here in the forest lays claim to you.
A most wicked Sir Oliver, Audrey, a most vile Martext. But Audrey, there's a young man here in the forest who claims you.
Ay, I know who 'tis. He hath no interest in me in the world.
Yes, I know who it is. He has no claim on me at all.
Here comes the man you mean.
Here comes the man you mean.
It is meat and drink to me to see a clown. By my troth, we that have / good wits have much to answer for. We shall be flouting; we cannot / hold.
It's food and drink to me to see a country bumpkin. Honestly, we who have good wits have a lot to answer for. We have to mock; we can't help ourselves.
God give you good evening, William.
And good ev'n to you, sir.
And good evening to you, sir.
Good ev'n, gentle friend. Cover thy head, cover thy head. Nay, prithee, / be covered. How old are you, friend?
Good evening, gentle friend. Put your hat on, put your hat on. No, please, keep it on. How old are you, friend?
A ripe age. Is thy name William?
A ripe age. Is your name William?
A fair name. Wast born i' th' forest here?
A fine name. Were you born here in the forest?
"Thank God." A good answer. Art rich?
'Thank God.' A good answer. Are you rich?
"So-so" is good, very good, very excellent good. And yet it is not, it / is but so-so. Art thou wise?
'So-so' is good, very good, very excellently good. And yet it isn't; it's only so-so. Are you wise?
Ay, sir, I have a pretty wit.
Yes, sir, I've got quite a good wit.

Why, thou sayst well. I do now remember a saying: "The fool doth think / he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool." The heathen / philosopher, when he had a desire to eat a grape, would open his lips / when he put it into his mouth, meaning thereby that grapes were made to / eat and lips to open. You do love this maid?

Why, well said. I remember now a saying: 'The fool thinks he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool.' The heathen philosopher, when he wanted to eat a grape, would open his lips when he put it into his mouth, meaning by that that grapes were made to be eaten and lips to be opened. You love this girl?
Give me your hand. Art thou learned?
Give me your hand. Are you educated?

Then learn this of me: to have is to have. For it is a figure in / rhetoric that drink, being poured out of cup into a glass, by filling / the one doth empty the other. For all your writers do consent that / ipse is "he." Now, you are not ipse, for I am he.

Then learn this from me: to have is to have. Because it's a figure of speech that drink, when it's poured out of a cup into a glass, fills one by emptying the other. Because all writers agree that ipse means 'he'. Now, you are not ipse, because I am he.

He, sir, that must marry this woman. Therefore, you clown, / abandon—which is in the vulgar, "leave"—the society—which in the / boorish is "company"—of this female—which in the common is "woman"; / which together is, abandon the society of this female, or, clown, thou / perishest; or, to thy better understanding, diest; or, to wit, I kill / thee, make thee away, translate thy life into death, thy liberty into / bondage. I will deal in poison with thee, or in bastinado, or in steel. / I will bandy with thee in faction; will o'errun thee with policy. I / will kill thee a hundred and fifty ways! Therefore tremble and depart.

The he, sir, who's going to marry this woman. So, you bumpkin, abandon (which is to say in the vulgar tongue 'leave') the society (which in the peasant tongue is 'company') of this female (which in the common tongue is 'woman'). Put together: abandon the society of this female, or, bumpkin, you perish; or, to help you understand, you die; that is to say, I kill you, do away with you, translate your life into death, your liberty into bondage. I'll deal with you with poison, or a beating, or a sword. I'll fight you with a gang; I'll overwhelm you with cunning. I'll kill you a hundred and fifty ways! So tremble and go.
Our master and mistress seek you. Come away, away.
Our master and mistress are looking for you. Come along, come along.
Trip, Audrey, trip, Audrey! I attend, I attend.
Skip along, Audrey, skip along, Audrey! I'm coming, I'm coming.
Is't possible that on so little acquaintance you should like her? That / but seeing, you should love her? And loving woo? And wooing, she should / grant? And will you persever to enjoy her?

Is it possible that, knowing her so little, you should like her? That just by seeing her, you should love her? And loving her, woo her? And when you wooed, she said yes? And will you go through with it and marry her?

Neither call the giddiness of it in question, the poverty of her, the / small acquaintance, my sudden wooing, nor her sudden consenting. But / say with me, I love Aliena; say with her that she loves me; consent / with both that we may enjoy each other. It shall be to your good, for / my father's house and all the revenue that was old Sir Rowland's will I / estate upon you, and here live and die a shepherd.

Don't question how dizzy-fast it's been, or her poverty, or how little we know each other, or my sudden wooing, or her sudden consent. Just agree with me that I love Aliena; agree with her that she loves me; agree with us both that we should have each other. It'll be to your advantage, because I'll make over to you our father's house and all the income that belonged to old Sir Rowland, and live and die here as a shepherd.
You have my consent. Let your wedding be tomorrow. Thither will I / invite the Duke and all's contented followers. Go you and prepare / Aliena; for, look you, here comes my Rosalind.
You have my consent. Let your wedding be tomorrow. I'll invite the Duke and all his contented followers. Go and get Aliena ready; because, look, here comes my Rosalind.
O my dear Orlando, how it grieves me to see thee wear thy heart in a / scarf!
Oh, my dear Orlando, it grieves me so much to see you wearing your heart in a sling!
I thought thy heart had been wounded with the claws of a lion.
I thought your heart had been wounded by a lion's claws.
Wounded it is, but with the eyes of a lady.
It is wounded, but by a lady's eyes.
Did your brother tell you how I counterfeited to swoon when he showed / me your handkercher?
Did your brother tell you how I faked a faint when he showed me your handkerchief?
Ay, and greater wonders than that.
Yes, and greater wonders than that.

O, I know where you are. Nay, 'tis true. There was never anything so / sudden but the fight of two rams, and Caesar's thrasonical brag of "I / came, saw and overcame." For your brother and my sister no sooner met / but they looked; no sooner looked but they loved; no sooner loved but / they sighed; no sooner sighed but they asked one another the reason; no / sooner knew the reason but they sought the remedy; and in these degrees / have they made pair of stairs to marriage, which they will climb / incontinent, or else be incontinent before marriage. They are in the / very wrath of love, and they will together. Clubs cannot part them.

Oh, I know what you mean. Yes, it's true. There was never anything so sudden, except a fight between two rams, and Caesar's boastful 'I came, I saw, I conquered.' Because your brother and my sister no sooner met than they looked; no sooner looked than they loved; no sooner loved than they sighed; no sooner sighed than they asked each other why; no sooner knew why than they looked for the cure. And with these steps they've built a pair of stairs to marriage, which they'll climb straight away, or else be unchaste before marriage. They're in the very frenzy of love, and they'll come together. Clubs couldn't separate them.

They shall be married tomorrow, and I will bid the Duke to the nuptial. / But O, how bitter a thing it is to look into happiness through another / man's eyes! By so much the more shall I tomorrow be at the height of / heart-heaviness, by how much I shall think my brother happy in having / what he wishes for.

They'll be married tomorrow, and I'll invite the Duke to the wedding. But oh, how bitter it is to look at happiness through another man's eyes! The happier I think my brother is in having what he wants, the heavier my heart will be tomorrow.
Why, then, tomorrow I cannot serve your turn for Rosalind?
Why, then, can't I stand in for Rosalind tomorrow?
I can live no longer by thinking.
I can't live on make-believe any longer.

I will weary you then no longer with idle talking. Know of me then—for / now I speak to some purpose—that I know you are a gentleman of good / conceit. I speak not this that you should bear a good opinion of my / knowledge, insomuch I say I know you are. Neither do I labour for a / greater esteem than may in some little measure draw a belief from you, / to do yourself good, and not to grace me. Believe then, if you please, / that I can do strange things. I have, since I was three year old, / conversed with a magician, most profound in his art and yet not / damnable. If you do love Rosalind so near the heart as your gesture / cries it out, when your brother marries Aliena shall you marry her. I / know into what straits of fortune she is driven and it is not / impossible to me, if it appear not inconvenient to you, to set her / before your eyes tomorrow, human as she is, and without any danger.

Then I won't tire you any more with idle talk. Listen to me, then, because now I'm speaking seriously. I know you're a gentleman of good understanding. I don't say this so that you'll think highly of my knowledge because I say I know you are. Nor am I trying to win more respect than will make you believe me a little, to do yourself good, not to flatter me. So believe, if you like, that I can do strange things. Since I was three years old I've been in contact with a magician, very deep in his art, but not wicked. If you love Rosalind as deeply as your behaviour shows, then when your brother marries Aliena you'll marry her. I know what difficult circumstances she's been driven into, and it's not impossible for me, if you don't object, to set her in front of your eyes tomorrow, in her own human form and without any danger.

By my life, I do, which I tender dearly, though I say I am a magician. / Therefore put you in your best array, bid your friends; for if you will / be married tomorrow, you shall, and to Rosalind, if you will.

On my life I am, which I value dearly, even though I say I'm a magician. So put on your best clothes and invite your friends; because if you want to be married tomorrow, you will be, and to Rosalind, if you like.
Look, here comes a lover of mine and a lover of hers.
Look, here comes a lover of mine and a lover of hers.
Youth, you have done me much ungentleness / To show the letter that I writ to you.
Youth, you've been very unkind to me in showing the letter I wrote you.
I care not if I have; it is my study / To seem despiteful and ungentle to you. / You are there followed by a faithful shepherd. / Look upon him, love him; he worships you.
I don't care if I have. I make a point of seeming spiteful and unkind to you. You're followed there by a faithful shepherd. Look at him, love him; he worships you.
Good shepherd, tell this youth what 'tis to love.
Good shepherd, tell this youth what it is to love.
It is to be all made of sighs and tears, / And so am I for Phoebe.
It's to be made entirely of sighs and tears; and that's what I am for Phoebe.
It is to be all made of faith and service, / And so am I for Phoebe.
It's to be made entirely of faithfulness and service; and that's what I am for Phoebe.

It is to be all made of fantasy, / All made of passion, and all made of wishes, / All adoration, duty, and observance, / All humbleness, all patience, and impatience, / All purity, all trial, all observance, / And so am I for Phoebe.

It's to be made entirely of fancy, entirely of passion and entirely of wishes, all adoration, duty and devotion, all humility, all patience and impatience, all purity, all suffering, all obedience; and that's what I am for Phoebe.
And so am I for Ganymede.
And so am I for Ganymede.
And so am I for Rosalind.
And so am I for Rosalind.
And so am I for no woman.
And so am I for no woman.
[To Rosalind] If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
If that's so, why do you blame me for loving you?
[To Phoebe] If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
If that's so, why do you blame me for loving you?
If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
If that's so, why do you blame me for loving you?
Why do you speak too, "Why blame you me to love you?"
Who are you saying it to, 'Why do you blame me for loving you'?
To her that is not here, nor doth not hear.
To her who isn't here, and can't hear.

Pray you, no more of this, 'tis like the howling of Irish wolves / against the moon. / [To Silvius] I will help you if I can. / [To Phoebe] I would love you if I could.—Tomorrow meet me all / together. / [To Phoebe] I will marry you, if ever I marry woman, and I'll be / married tomorrow. / [To Orlando] I will satisfy you if ever I satisfied man, and you / shall be married tomorrow. / [To Silvius] I will content you, if what pleases you contents you, / and you shall be married tomorrow. / [To Orlando] As you love Rosalind, meet. / [To Silvius] As you love Phoebe, meet.—And as I love no woman, I'll / meet. So fare you well. I have left you commands.

Please, no more of this; it's like Irish wolves howling at the moon. I'll help you if I can. I'd love you if I could. Tomorrow, all of you meet me together. I'll marry you, if I ever marry a woman, and I'll be married tomorrow. I'll satisfy you, if I ever satisfied a man, and you'll be married tomorrow. I'll make you happy, if what pleases you makes you happy, and you'll be married tomorrow. As you love Rosalind, meet me. As you love Phoebe, meet me. And as I love no woman, I'll be there. So goodbye. I've given you your orders.
I'll not fail, if I live.
I won't fail, if I'm alive.
Tomorrow is the joyful day, Audrey, tomorrow will we be married.
Tomorrow is the happy day, Audrey. Tomorrow we'll be married.
I do desire it with all my heart; and I hope it is no dishonest desire / to desire to be a woman of the world.
I want it with all my heart, and I hope it's not an immodest wish to want to be a married woman.
Here come two of the banished Duke's pages.
Here come two of the banished Duke's pages.
Good to see you, honest gentleman.
By my troth, well met. Come sit, sit, and a song.
Truly, good to see you. Come and sit, sit, and give us a song.
We are for you, sit i' th' middle.
We're ready for you. Sit in the middle.
Shall we clap into't roundly, without hawking or spitting or saying we / are hoarse, which are the only prologues to a bad voice?
Shall we launch straight into it, without clearing our throats or spitting or saying we're hoarse, which are the usual introductions to a bad voice?
I'faith, i'faith, and both in a tune like two gipsies on a horse.
Yes, yes, and both in the same tune, like two gypsies riding one horse.

[Sing] / It was a lover and his lass, / With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, / That o'er the green cornfield did pass / In the spring-time, the only pretty ring time, / When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding. / Sweet lovers love the spring. / Between the acres of the rye, / With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, / These pretty country folks would lie, / In the spring-time, the only pretty ring time, / When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding. / Sweet lovers love the spring. / This carol they began that hour, / With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, / How that a life was but a flower, / In the spring-time, the only pretty ring time, / When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding. / Sweet lovers love the spring. / And therefore take the present time, / With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, / For love is crowned with the prime, / In the spring-time, the only pretty ring time, / When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding. / Sweet lovers love the spring.

It was a lover and his girl, with a hey and a ho and a hey nonino, who walked across the green cornfield in springtime, the only pretty wedding-ring time, when birds sing, hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring. Between the strips of rye, with a hey and a ho and a hey nonino, these pretty country people would lie down, in springtime, the only pretty wedding-ring time, when birds sing, hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring. They began this song at that hour, with a hey and a ho and a hey nonino, about how life is only a flower, in springtime, the only pretty wedding-ring time, when birds sing, hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring. So seize the present time, with a hey and a ho and a hey nonino, because love is crowned in its springtime, in springtime, the only pretty wedding-ring time, when birds sing, hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring.
Truly, young gentlemen, though there was no great matter in the ditty, / yet the note was very untuneable.
Truly, young gentlemen, though there wasn't much meaning in the song, the tune was very untuneful.
You are deceived, sir, we kept time, we lost not our time.
You're mistaken, sir. We kept time; we didn't lose our time.
By my troth, yes. I count it but time lost to hear such a foolish song. / God be wi' you, and God mend your voices. Come, Audrey.
Truly, you did. I count it as time lost listening to such a foolish song. God be with you, and God improve your voices. Come, Audrey.
Dost thou believe, Orlando, that the boy / Can do all this that he hath promised?
Do you believe, Orlando, that the boy can do everything he's promised?
I sometimes do believe and sometimes do not, / As those that fear they hope, and know they fear.
Sometimes I believe it and sometimes I don't, like people who are afraid to hope, and know they're afraid.
Patience once more whiles our compact is urged. / [To the Duke] You say, if I bring in your Rosalind, / You will bestow her on Orlando here?
Be patient once more while our agreement is confirmed. You say that if I bring in your Rosalind, you'll give her to Orlando here?
That would I, had I kingdoms to give with her.
I would, even if I had kingdoms to give with her.
[To Orlando] And you say you will have her when I bring her?
And you say you'll have her when I bring her?
That would I, were I of all kingdoms king.
I would, even if I were king of all the kingdoms.
[To Phoebe] You say you'll marry me if I be willing?
You say you'll marry me if I'm willing?
That will I, should I die the hour after.
I will, even if I died an hour afterwards.
But if you do refuse to marry me, / You'll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd?
But if you refuse to marry me, you'll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd?
[To Silvius] You say that you'll have Phoebe if she will?
You say that you'll have Phoebe if she's willing?
Though to have her and death were both one thing.
Even if having her and dying were the same thing.

I have promised to make all this matter even. / Keep you your word, O Duke, to give your daughter, / You yours, Orlando, to receive his daughter. / Keep your word, Phoebe, that you'll marry me, / Or else, refusing me, to wed this shepherd. / Keep your word, Silvius, that you'll marry her / If she refuse me. And from hence I go / To make these doubts all even.

I've promised to settle this whole business. You keep your word, Duke, to give your daughter away; you yours, Orlando, to take his daughter. Keep your word, Phoebe, that you'll marry me, or else, if you refuse me, marry this shepherd. Keep your word, Silvius, that you'll marry her if she refuses me. And now I'm going to settle all these doubts.
I do remember in this shepherd boy / Some lively touches of my daughter's favour.
I seem to see in this shepherd boy some lively traces of my daughter's looks.

My lord, the first time that I ever saw him / Methought he was a brother to your daughter. / But, my good lord, this boy is forest-born / And hath been tutored in the rudiments / Of many desperate studies by his uncle, / Whom he reports to be a great magician, / Obscured in the circle of this forest.

My lord, the first time I ever saw him I thought he was your daughter's brother. But, my good lord, this boy was born in the forest, and has been taught the basics of many dangerous arts by his uncle, who he says is a great magician, hidden within the bounds of this forest.
There is sure another flood toward, and these couples are coming to the / ark. Here comes a pair of very strange beasts, which in all tongues are / called fools.
There must be another Flood coming, and these couples are going into the ark. Here comes a pair of very strange animals, which in every language are called fools.
Salutation and greeting to you all.
Salutations and greetings to you all.
Good my lord, bid him welcome. This is the motley-minded gentleman that / I have so often met in the forest. He hath been a courtier, he swears.
My good lord, welcome him. This is the motley-minded gentleman I've so often met in the forest. He swears he's been a courtier.

If any man doubt that, let him put me to my purgation. I have trod a / measure; I have flattered a lady; I have been politic with my friend, / smooth with mine enemy; I have undone three tailors; I have had four / quarrels, and like to have fought one.

If anyone doubts it, let him put me to the test. I've danced a stately dance; I've flattered a lady; I've been cunning with my friend and smooth with my enemy; I've ruined three tailors by not paying them; I've had four quarrels, and nearly fought one of them.
And how was that ta'en up?
Faith, we met, and found the quarrel was upon the seventh cause.
Well, we met, and found the quarrel was on the seventh cause.
How seventh cause?—Good my lord, like this fellow?
What do you mean, the seventh cause? My good lord, don't you like this fellow?

God 'ild you, sir, I desire you of the like. I press in here, sir, / amongst the rest of the country copulatives, to swear and to forswear / according as marriage binds and blood breaks. A poor virgin, sir, an / ill-favoured thing, sir, but mine own; a poor humour of mine, sir, to / take that that no man else will. Rich honesty dwells like a miser, sir, / in a poor house, as your pearl in your foul oyster.

God reward you, sir; I hope you'll go on liking me. I push in here, sir, among the rest of these country couples, to swear and break my oath, as marriage binds and passion breaks. A poor virgin, sir, an ugly thing, sir, but my own. It's a poor whim of mine, sir, to take what no one else will. Rich chastity lives like a miser, sir, in a poor house, like a pearl in an ugly oyster.
By my faith, he is very swift and sententious.
Honestly, he's very quick and full of wise sayings.
According to the fool's bolt, sir, and such dulcet diseases.
As the fool's arrow goes, sir, quick and soon spent, and such sweet diseases.
But, for the seventh cause. How did you find the quarrel on the seventh / cause?
But about the seventh cause. How did you find the quarrel was on the seventh cause?

Upon a lie seven times removed—bear your body more seeming, Audrey—as / thus, sir. I did dislike the cut of a certain courtier's beard. He sent / me word if I said his beard was not cut well, he was in the mind it / was. This is called the "retort courteous". If I sent him word again it / was not well cut, he would send me word he cut it to please himself. / This is called the "quip modest". If again it was not well cut, he / disabled my judgement. This is called the "reply churlish". If again it / was not well cut, he would answer I spake not true. This is called the / "reproof valiant". If again it was not well cut, he would say I lie. / This is called the "countercheck quarrelsome", and so, to the "lie / circumstantial", and the "lie direct".

On a lie seven times removed. (Stand up straighter, Audrey.) Like this, sir. I didn't like the cut of a certain courtier's beard. He sent me word that if I said his beard wasn't well cut, he was of the opinion that it was. This is called the 'retort courteous'. If I sent him word again that it wasn't well cut, he'd send me word that he cut it to please himself. This is called the 'quip modest'. If again it wasn't well cut, he'd say my judgment was no good. This is called the 'reply churlish'. If again it wasn't well cut, he'd answer that I wasn't telling the truth. This is called the 'reproof valiant'. If again it wasn't well cut, he'd say I lie. This is called the 'countercheck quarrelsome'. And so on to the 'lie circumstantial' and the 'lie direct'.
And how oft did you say his beard was not well cut?
And how many times did you say his beard wasn't well cut?
I durst go no further than the lie circumstantial, nor he durst not / give me the lie direct; and so we measured swords and parted.
I didn't dare go further than the lie circumstantial, and he didn't dare give me the lie direct; so we measured swords and went our separate ways.
Can you nominate in order now the degrees of the lie?
Can you name the degrees of the lie in order now?

O sir, we quarrel in print, by the book, as you have books for good / manners. I will name you the degrees: the first, the retort courteous; / the second, the quip modest; the third, the reply churlish; the fourth, / the reproof valiant; the fifth, the countercheck quarrelsome; the / sixth, the lie with circumstance; the seventh, the lie direct. All / these you may avoid but the lie direct and you may avoid that too with / an "if". I knew when seven justices could not take up a quarrel, but / when the parties were met themselves, one of them thought but of an / "if", as, "if you said so, then I said so;" and they shook hands, and / swore brothers. Your "if" is the only peacemaker; much virtue in "if."

Oh, sir, we quarrel by the printed rule book, just as you have books of good manners. I'll name the degrees for you. The first, the retort courteous; the second, the quip modest; the third, the reply churlish; the fourth, the reproof valiant; the fifth, the countercheck quarrelsome; the sixth, the lie with circumstance; the seventh, the lie direct. You can avoid all of them except the lie direct, and you can avoid that too with an 'if'. I've known seven judges fail to settle a quarrel, but when the two men met, one of them just thought of an 'if', like 'If you said so, then I said so', and they shook hands and swore to be brothers. Your 'if' is the only peacemaker. There's great power in 'if'.
Is not this a rare fellow, my lord? He's as good at anything, and yet a / fool.
Isn't this an extraordinary fellow, my lord? He's good at everything, and yet he's a fool.
He uses his folly like a stalking-horse, and under the presentation of / that he shoots his wit.
He uses his foolery like a stalking-horse, and hidden behind it he shoots his wit.

Then is there mirth in heaven / When earthly things made even / Atone together. / Good Duke, receive thy daughter. / Hymen from heaven brought her, / Yea, brought her hither, / That thou mightst join her hand with his, / Whose heart within his bosom is.

Then there is joy in heaven, when earthly things are set right and made one. Good Duke, receive your daughter. Hymen brought her from heaven, yes, brought her here, so that you could join her hand with his, whose heart she holds in her own breast.
[To Duke Senior] To you I give myself, for I am yours. / [To Orlando] To you I give myself, for I am yours.
To you I give myself, because I am yours. To you I give myself, because I am yours.
If there be truth in sight, you are my daughter.
If my eyes tell the truth, you're my daughter.
If there be truth in sight, you are my Rosalind.
If my eyes tell the truth, you're my Rosalind.
If sight and shape be true, / Why then, my love adieu.
If what I see is true, then, my love, goodbye.
[To Duke Senior] I'll have no father, if you be not he. / [To Orlando] I'll have no husband, if you be not he. / [To Phoebe] Nor ne'er wed woman, if you be not she.
I'll have no father, if you're not he. I'll have no husband, if you're not he. And I'll never marry a woman, if you're not she.

Peace, ho! I bar confusion. / 'Tis I must make conclusion / Of these most strange events. / Here's eight that must take hands / To join in Hymen's bands, / If truth holds true contents. / [To Orlando and Rosalind] You and you no cross shall part. / [To Celia and Oliver] You and you are heart in heart. / [To Phoebe] You to his love must accord / Or have a woman to your lord. / [To Audrey and Touchstone] You and you are sure together / As the winter to foul weather. / Whiles a wedlock hymn we sing, / Feed yourselves with questioning, / That reason wonder may diminish / How thus we met, and these things finish. / [Song] / Wedding is great Juno's crown, / O blessed bond of board and bed. / 'Tis Hymen peoples every town, / High wedlock then be honoured. / Honour, high honour, and renown / To Hymen, god of every town.

Quiet! I forbid confusion. It's for me to bring these very strange events to an end. Here are eight people who must take hands and be joined in marriage, if truth is truly what it seems. You and you no trouble shall part. You and you are heart in heart. You must agree to his love, or have a woman for your husband. You and you are as sure to be together as winter is to bad weather. While we sing a wedding hymn, satisfy yourselves with questions, so that reason may lessen your wonder at how we met and how these things end. Marriage is great Juno's crown, oh blessed bond of table and bed. It's Hymen who fills every town with people, so let marriage be highly honoured. Honour, high honour and fame to Hymen, god of every town.
O my dear niece, welcome thou art to me / Even daughter, welcome in no less degree.
Oh, my dear niece, you're as welcome to me as a daughter, welcome no less.
[To Silvius] I will not eat my word, now thou art mine, / Thy faith my fancy to thee doth combine.
I won't go back on my word, now you're mine. Your faithfulness binds my love to you.

Let me have audience for a word or two. / I am the second son of old Sir Rowland, / That bring these tidings to this fair assembly. / Duke Frederick, hearing how that every day / Men of great worth resorted to this forest, / Addressed a mighty power, which were on foot / In his own conduct, purposely to take / His brother here and put him to the sword; / And to the skirts of this wild wood he came, / Where, meeting with an old religious man, / After some question with him, was converted / Both from his enterprise and from the world, / His crown bequeathing to his banished brother, / And all their lands restored to them again / That were with him exiled. This to be true / I do engage my life.

Let me have a hearing for a word or two. I'm the second son of old Sir Rowland, and I bring this news to this fine gathering. Duke Frederick, hearing that men of great worth were coming to this forest every day, raised a mighty army and set out at its head, with the aim of capturing his brother here and putting him to the sword. He came to the edge of this wild wood, and there he met an old religious man, and after some talk with him was converted, both from his plan and from the world. He is handing his crown to his banished brother, and restoring all their lands to those who were exiled with him. I stake my life that this is true.

Welcome, young man. / Thou offer'st fairly to thy brother's wedding: / To one his lands withheld, and to the other / A land itself at large, a potent dukedom. / First, in this forest let us do those ends / That here were well begun and well begot; / And after, every of this happy number / That have endured shrewd days and nights with us / Shall share the good of our returned fortune, / According to the measure of their states. / Meantime, forget this new-fall'n dignity, / And fall into our rustic revelry. / Play, music! And you brides and bridegrooms all, / With measure heaped in joy to th' measures fall.

Welcome, young man. You bring a fine gift to your brothers' weddings: to one, his lands that were withheld from him, and to the other, a whole land, a powerful dukedom. First, let's finish here in this forest what was well begun and well conceived here. And afterwards, every one of this happy group who has lived through hard days and nights with us will share in the good of our restored fortune, each according to his rank. Meanwhile, forget this newly arrived greatness, and join in our country celebrations. Play, music! And all you brides and bridegrooms, step out to the dances with your cups of joy heaped full.
Sir, by your patience. If I heard you rightly, / The Duke hath put on a religious life / And thrown into neglect the pompous court.
Sir, with your permission. If I heard you right, the Duke has taken up a religious life and abandoned the splendid court.

To him will I. Out of these convertites / There is much matter to be heard and learned. / [To Duke Senior] You to your former honour I bequeath; / Your patience and your virtue well deserves it. / [To Orlando] You to a love that your true faith doth merit. / [To Oliver] You to your land, and love, and great allies. / [To Silvius] You to a long and well-deserved bed. / [To Touchstone] And you to wrangling, for thy loving voyage / Is but for two months victualled.—So to your pleasures, / I am for other than for dancing measures.

I'll go to him. There's a lot to be heard and learned from these converts. You I leave to your former honour; your patience and your goodness deserve it. You, to a love your true faithfulness has earned. You, to your land and love and powerful in-laws. You, to a long and well-deserved marriage bed. And you to squabbling, because your loving voyage has only two months' supplies on board. So, enjoy yourselves; I'm meant for other things than dancing.
To see no pastime, I. What you would have / I'll stay to know at your abandoned cave.
I won't stay to watch your amusements. Whatever you want of me, I'll wait to hear at the cave you've left behind.
Proceed, proceed! We will begin these rites, / As we do trust they'll end, in true delights.
Go on, go on! We'll begin these ceremonies as we trust they'll end, in true delight.

It is not the fashion to see the lady the epilogue, but it is no more / unhandsome than to see the lord the prologue. If it be true that good / wine needs no bush, 'tis true that a good play needs no epilogue. Yet / to good wine they do use good bushes, and good plays prove the better / by the help of good epilogues. What a case am I in then, that am / neither a good epilogue nor cannot insinuate with you in the behalf of / a good play! I am not furnished like a beggar; therefore to beg will / not become me. My way is to conjure you, and I'll begin with the women. / I charge you, O women, for the love you bear to men, to like as much of / this play as please you. And I charge you, O men, for the love you bear / to women—as I perceive by your simpering, none of you hates them—that / between you and the women the play may please. If I were a woman, I / would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me, complexions / that liked me, and breaths that I defied not. And I am sure as many as / have good beards, or good faces, or sweet breaths will for my kind / offer, when I make curtsy, bid me farewell.

It's not the custom to see the lady speak the epilogue, but it's no more unsuitable than seeing the lord speak the prologue. If it's true that good wine needs no advertising, it's true that a good play needs no epilogue. But they do advertise good wine, and good plays turn out better with the help of good epilogues. What a situation I'm in, then, being neither a good epilogue nor able to win you over on behalf of a good play! I'm not dressed like a beggar, so begging won't suit me. My way is to cast a spell on you, and I'll begin with the women. I order you, women, by the love you have for men, to like as much of this play as pleases you. And I order you, men, by the love you have for women (and I can see by your simpering that none of you hates them), that between you and the women the play may please. If I were a woman, I'd kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me, complexions that I liked and breath that didn't repel me. And I'm sure that as many as have good beards or good faces or sweet breath will, in return for my kind offer, say goodbye to me with applause when I curtsy.
